entry.title: Record, replay, fork: debugging an agent that failed mid-run
entry.summary: Reza Amini (Flashback) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on saving agent runs as cassettes so you can rewind to the bad step and fork a fix instead of re-running.
entry.content:
Logs tell you an agent broke. They do not hand you the run back. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Reza Amini, Senior Software Engineer at Flashback, argues for a habit that will look familiar to anyone who has used HTTP test fixtures: record the full agent run as a cassette, replay it to find the bad step, then fork from that step with a fix.

The expensive default: run it all again

Multi-step agents fail in the middle. A bad tool call, a wrong intermediate answer, a broken handoff between steps. The usual response is to re-run the whole thing and hope the failure shows up again. Reza lists what that costs: more time, more tokens, and the same live side effects again.

That last item is the one that should worry you. If step three sent an email or wrote to a database, re-running the pipeline to debug step seven sends the email again. Nobody wants to explain to a customer that they got three identical messages because someone was investigating a parsing bug.

And non-determinism makes it worse. The second run may take a different path entirely, succeed, and leave you with a bug you can no longer see.

A cassette is a run you can hold

The proposal is simple enough to fit on a sticky note: record, replay, fork.

  • Record the full run locally as a cassette: prompts, tool calls and their results.
  • Replay the same steps exactly, so you can walk to the point where it went wrong.
  • Fork from that step with a change, and check the fix before you touch production again.

If you have used VCR-style fixtures for HTTP tests, the shape will be familiar. The twist is applying it to a whole agent trajectory, where the "responses" include model outputs that you could never reproduce by calling the model again.

Reza draws a clean line between this and tracing. Traces help you observe a run. A cassette lets you reproduce it and change one decision. They sit next to each other in your toolkit, alongside logs and plain re-runs, rather than replacing anything.

The demo: rewind, fork, recover

The talk includes a live demo of a failed multi-step agent run. Reza rewinds to the bad step, forks a fix, and shows the recovery without re-running the whole pipeline. That is the part to watch closely, because the interesting questions are in the details: what exactly gets captured, and what happens to the steps after the fork.

Honest scope

Reza works at Flashback, and Flashback is one way to keep these cassettes. The abstract is upfront that the session teaches the habit and is not a product pitch, so expect the pattern first and the tool as one possible implementation.

Who should watch

Engineers who own agents with side effects: anything that writes, sends, books or pays. Also anyone who has burned a pile of tokens re-running a twenty-step workflow to look at step nineteen. If your agents are read-only chatbots, the payoff is smaller, though the reproducibility argument still applies.

Related Conf42 talks

  • Feature Flags as Incident Evidence: Safer AI-Assisted RCA Workflows by Ishan Shah, on keeping AI-assisted incident analysis grounded in evidence.
  • You Can't Debug What You Can't See: Observability for AI Agents by Sabith K Soopy, the tracing side Reza wants cassettes to sit next to.
  • Three Hours Debugging Code I Never Wrote by Artemis Leonardou, a debugging story from the agent-written-code end.

Watch Reza Amini's talk at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19.

entry.title: Your LangGraph.js agent works. Can it survive a restart?
entry.summary: Maina Wycliffe (Garatropic) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 introduces skein-js, a self-hosted runtime for LangGraph.js agents that pause, retry and restart.
entry.content:
An agent that pauses for human approval has to outlive the human's lunch break, a deploy and a server restart. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Maina Wycliffe, founder and chief builder at Garatropic, introduces skein-js, an open-source, self-hosted TypeScript server runtime that gives LangGraph.js agents the infrastructure to do exactly that.

The scenario that breaks most agent demos

Maina opens with a story every ops person will recognise. An agent reviews a support ticket, proposes an action, and pauses for approval. The reviewer comes back tomorrow. In the meantime the server has restarted, a new version has been deployed, and the system that submitted the request has retried it.

Three things now have to be true. The approval request must still exist. The retry must resolve to the original piece of work instead of spawning a twin. And an operator needs to be able to understand what happened. Building a useful agent is the start; running it as a dependable service is the rest of the job.

LangGraph runs the graph, skein-js runs the service

The division of labour is clear. LangGraph already provides graph execution, checkpointing and interrupts. skein-js supplies what sits around those graphs in production: persistent API resources, background execution, streaming, and an operator console. Importantly for anyone with code already written, it keeps existing LangGraph.js graphs and SDK clients working.

So this is not a new agent framework. It is closer to the application server you wish had shipped with the framework you already use. Self-hosted, which matters if your agents touch data that is not allowed to leave your infrastructure.

Postgres for memory, Redis for the work queue

The talk follows an issue-triage workflow through three failures: a duplicate submission, a human approval step, and a server restart. Along the way Maina shows how Postgres persistence and Redis-backed background work support reliable execution.

The part worth paying attention to is where Maina marks the limits. The abstract promises a look at where idempotency guarantees end. That is refreshingly honest. Every durable execution system has a boundary past which "exactly once" turns back into "at least once, good luck", and knowing where that line sits is more useful than a slide claiming there is none.

Telemetry closes the loop: when something does fail, the operator console and traces should explain why.

A checklist you can use on any runtime

Even if you never install skein-js, the failure scenarios are a portable test suite. Restart the server mid-approval. Retry the same request twice. Deploy a new version while a run is paused. Ask your current agent runtime to survive those, and you will learn a lot about it in an afternoon.

Who should watch

TypeScript teams on LangGraph.js who are moving agents from a notebook-shaped prototype to something that runs all week. Anyone building human-in-the-loop flows where approvals take hours or days. Python-only shops can still take the failure scenarios home; the runtime itself is JavaScript land.

Related Conf42 talks

  • Orchestrating Agentic State Machines with LangGraph: Learnings from Automating clinical documentation by Rajeshwari Sah, LangGraph in a regulated domain.
  • Reliable API Support: Human-in-the-Loop Agentic RAG for SRE by Vishal Shah, more on keeping a human in the loop.
  • Enhancing Workflow Reliability with Dapr: Techniques to Minimize Failure Costs by Siri Varma Vegiraju, durable workflows outside the agent world.

Watch Maina Wycliffe's talk at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19.

entry.title: Multi-agent systems need protocols before they need more agents
entry.summary: Daniel Akhabue (Qucoon) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on typed messages, retries, dead-letter queues and tracing for agents that talk to agents.
entry.content:
Four agents passing free text to each other is a distributed system with no schema, and it fails like one. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Daniel Akhabue, Senior AI Engineer at Qucoon, treats agent-to-agent communication as protocol engineering: typed messages, validation at every hop, retries, dead-letter queues and traces you can actually follow.

The session is built as a hands-on walkthrough. Instead of a slide of boxes and arrows, you build one: a small distributed system with a research agent that gathers information, an analysis agent that processes it, a synthesis agent that writes the report, and a validation agent that checks quality before anything leaves the building.

The failure modes are old friends

The abstract lists what goes wrong when agents coordinate without rules: inconsistent outputs, silent failures, race conditions, and systems nobody can debug. If you have run microservices, every item on that list will feel familiar. The difference is that the payload is now produced by a model, so the message that arrives at the next agent may be well-formed English and still be garbage as data.

That is the core argument of the talk. Agents are services. Treat the messages between them with the same discipline you would give to an API contract, and a lot of the "AI is unpredictable" pain turns back into ordinary engineering.

Pydantic is the contract, validation is the bouncer

Daniel's protocol layer starts with structured messages defined in Pydantic, so every agent interaction is type-checked. On top of that sit validation layers designed to catch errors before they cascade. A malformed handoff from the research agent should die at the door of the analysis agent, with a clear error, instead of travelling three steps downstream and turning into a confident, wrong report.

Concurrency gets its own treatment: when several agents run at once, you need proper synchronisation, or you get the race conditions the abstract warns about. Think of it as the agent version of two cron jobs writing the same file.

Borrow the whole reliability toolbox

The part that should please SREs is how much of the classic distributed-systems kit makes the cut:

  • automatic retry logic on agent calls
  • dead-letter queues for messages that keep failing
  • circuit breakers for agents that are misbehaving
  • event-driven architecture for coordination
  • semantic versioning for protocol changes, so a new message shape does not break an older agent
  • OpenTelemetry for observable agent workflows

Versioning is the sleeper hit here. Prompts and agents change weekly in most teams, and nobody bumps a version number. Once agents exchange typed messages, a protocol change becomes something you can version, test and roll out like any other API change.

Testing the non-deterministic bits

The talk also covers testing strategies for non-deterministic systems, which is where most multi-agent projects quietly give up. Combined with typed messages and traces, you get a system where a test can assert on structure and behaviour even when the wording of each output changes run to run.

Who should watch

Engineers who already have one agent in production and a roadmap that says "add three more". Platform and SRE folks who will be paged when those agents start talking to each other. If you are still deciding whether you need agents at all, this is not the starting point; it assumes you are past that question and want blueprints and debugging tools.

Related Conf42 talks

  • Engineering Production-Grade Multi-Agent Systems in the Cloud by Sandeep Mannapur, a cloud-side view of the same problem.
  • Make Agents Observable: Tracing Decisions, Tool Calls and Recovery by Emerson Braun, for the tracing half of Daniel's toolbox.
  • From Monoliths to Microminds: Building Resilient AI Platforms with Multi-Agentic Architecture by Sidhanta Panigrahy, on the platform around many agents.

Watch Daniel Akhabue's talk at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19.

entry.title: Fifty Claude agents in production: let the AI suggest, code decide
entry.summary: Muhammad Haris Farooq (Ruby AI) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on running 50+ Bedrock agents: judges that see tool output, cache traps, and a 75% cost cut.
entry.content:
Getting one agent to work is the demo. Keeping fifty of them accurate, measurable and affordable is the job. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Muhammad Haris Farooq, AI Lead at Ruby AI, shares the patterns that survived running a platform of 50+ Claude agents on Amazon Bedrock for real customers every day.

The agents research companies and the people in them, then write briefings before sales calls. That is a useful workload to learn from: lots of tool calls, lots of web data, a human on the other end who will notice a wrong fact in front of a prospect. Haris promises real traces and numbers, and the abstract already gives a few of them.

Let the AI suggest, let the code decide

The first rule is a boundary. Scores, formatting and anything that changes a customer's data stay in normal code. The model proposes; deterministic code disposes. Haris gives two reasons, and both are boring in the best way: it is cheaper, and you can test it.

It is a good antidote to the reflex of asking the model to do everything, including the arithmetic.

A judge that can't see the evidence will fail the witness

Quality monitoring runs in two tiers: quick code checks on every run, and AI judges on a sample of about 1,500 runs a month. The lesson that comes with it is the most quotable thing in the abstract. A judge that cannot see what the agent saw marks correct answers as wrong. Giving the judge the tool results took one answer's score from 0.2 to 0.95.

If you run LLM-as-judge anywhere, that one number is worth the session. A judge grading an answer without the retrieved context is grading against its own memory, and its memory is not your customer's CRM.

Prompt caching breaks without telling you

Ruby cut cost per run by about 75%, and a big part of that came from prompt caching. The catch: caching also breaks silently. A date in the system prompt, or tools listed in a different order, is enough to miss the cache, and nothing throws an error. Your bill just goes up.

Haris will show how to catch that, including a limit he measured on live Bedrock. This is the kind of detail you only learn by staring at invoices, so it is nice to have someone else do the staring.

Parallel where it's independent

The last pattern is speed. Running independent agents in parallel cut the time to research a company from about 32 minutes to 11. Nothing exotic, just the observation that agents with no data dependency on each other should not wait in line.

Who should watch

Anyone with more than a handful of agents in production, or with a plan to get there this quarter. It is especially useful for teams on Bedrock or using Claude models with prompt caching, and for anyone who has set up an LLM judge and quietly wondered why its scores feel off. Haris promises a short checklist you can apply to your own agents the next day, which is exactly the right size for a talk like this.

Related Conf42 talks

  • The Retry Storm That Ate My Budget: Debugging the Hidden Cost Loops in Agentic AI by Yamini Rathamsetty and Karthik Akula, the cost side of agents from a different angle.
  • The Judge Problem: Why Your Agentic Verifier is Silently Rotting in Production by Vsevolod Voropaev, more on judges that drift.
  • Less Theater, More Engineering: A Production Claude Code + MCP Agent Pipeline at 80% Accuracy by Suneet Malhotra, another production Claude story with numbers.

Watch Muhammad Haris Farooq's talk at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19.

entry.title: AI gardening: agent context drifts, so prune it on purpose
entry.summary: Ishan Shah (PayPal) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on AI Gardening: treating context and memory in long-running agent workflows as production state you maintain.
entry.content:
Long-running agent workflows rarely crash. They drift. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Ishan Shah, Staff Software Engineer at PayPal, names the discipline for dealing with that: AI Gardening, the ongoing work of deciding what context gets into an agentic system, what expires, what is kept for audit, and when memory gets reset.

The failure that doesn't page anyone

The opening line of the abstract sets it up well: most AI demos are short, and production MLOps and agentic workflows are not. Over time, a long-running system accumulates instructions, retrieved documents, tool outputs, partial plans, stale assumptions and memory from earlier work.

None of that looks like a normal service failure. The system keeps responding. Tools keep working. Your dashboards stay green. The workflow just becomes slowly harder to reason about, because its context has wandered away from what anyone intended.

That is a nasty class of problem for an on-call engineer. There is no error to grep for, only behaviour that feels a bit off, and a transcript long enough to make you give up scrolling.

Gardening, not bulldozing

The metaphor earns its keep. You do not fix a garden once; you prune, weed and decide what stays. Ishan applies that to the operational environment around an LLM workflow once it moves past a single prompt. The questions he puts on the table:

  • What context is allowed into a workflow in the first place?
  • What should expire, and when?
  • What must be preserved for audit?
  • When should memory be scoped, and when should it be reset?
  • How do you detect contradictory instructions piling up?
  • How do you make working state inspectable during real engineering tasks?

He is careful about the goal. The point is not to make probabilistic systems pretend to be deterministic. The point is to make the environment around them maintainable, with bounded context windows, explicit memory ownership, reset boundaries, retrieval evaluation, artifact handoffs, and enough evidence that a human can understand why the system behaved the way it did.

Context is production input

The takeaway checklist is short and sharp. Treat context as production input, with the same suspicion you give to user data. Separate durable knowledge from temporary working state. Make memory auditable. Design reset paths before drift turns into a failure mode. And give humans a clear way to inspect state, instead of asking them to trust a transcript.

That last point is the one many teams skip. Telling someone to read the conversation log is homework, not an inspection tool. A system that exposes its working state directly is one you can actually operate.

Who should watch

Engineers running agents that live longer than a single request: coding agents on big tasks, research pipelines, anything with persistent memory. MLOps and platform people who will be asked to own those systems after the demo is over. If your LLM use is single-shot prompts, file this one for later.

Related Conf42 talks

  • Make Agents Remember the Right Context at the Right Time by Anannya Roy Chowdhury, the memory-design side of the same coin.
  • Make Agents Remember the Right Context at the Right Time by Anannya Roy Chowdhury, on choosing what an agent should recall and when.
  • Prompt Drift Kills: How to Make Prompts Stable by Sachin Gupta, drift seen from the prompt layer.

Ishan has spoken at Conf42 before, too: his Feature Flags as Incident Evidence talk from Conf42 Feature Flags 2026, on governing AI-assisted root cause analysis, is a good companion.

entry.title: LLMday Tel Aviv brings data engineering and AI agents to one room
entry.summary: LLMday Tel Aviv, November 17 at Microsoft Reactor - free talks from FalkorDB, groundcover, Komodor, Snyk and TeraSky on agents, graphs and data.
entry.content:
LLMday lands in Tel Aviv for the first time on November 17, 2026, at the Microsoft Reactor, with a one-track day where LLM talks sit right next to hard data engineering. Speakers come from FalkorDB, groundcover, Komodor, Cato Networks, Neradot, Snyk and TeraSky, and the event is free to attend (registration is with approval).

The edition is run with Microsoft and TeraSky, and the angle is the overlap: what happens to your agents when the data under them is huge, messy or impossible to summarise.

The lineup reads like a postmortem collection, in the good way

Several talks are about things that broke and what the team did next.

  • Avital Tamir (groundcover), The Ninth Rewrite Might Be a Delete: Building Production AI Agents on Shifting Ground. The abstract counts eight full rewrites of a production agent, some forced by mistakes, some by model and platform releases that turned the team's own infrastructure into somebody else's feature.
  • Nir Adler (Komodor), Bye Bye Timestream - A Tale of Migrating 5.9 Billion Metrics a Day to ClickHouse. When AWS announced end of life for Amazon Timestream, Komodor had to move the metrics behind customer dashboards without taking queries offline.
  • Liran Tal (Snyk), From Second Brain to AI Chief-of-Staff: Engineering an Assistant That Runs Your Workweek. A markdown second brain wired into email, chat, calendar and a work tracker, which looked tidy for six weeks while it was quietly failing.

Agents need a map, and sometimes the raw numbers

Roi Lipman (FalkorDB) takes on a familiar pain in From grep to graph: giving AI agents a map of your code: coding agents handle a single function fine, then fall back to grep when you ask what breaks if a shared type changes across many repos. His approach turns the codebase into a graph the agent can query.

Liza Katz (Neradot) goes the other way in Just Roll Up and Die: When Your Agent Needs Data You Can't Aggregate. In construction and manufacturing, averaging lies: 99% progress is meaningless if the missing 1% is a structural beam. The talk is an anonymised case study of building an LLM system on data you are not allowed to compress.

Noa Baron (Cato Networks) brings From Data Pipelines to Humans: Advantages of Mechanical Sympathy, on context switching as a cost for CPUs and for people alike. Yev Berman (TeraSky) opens the technical part with Talk to Your Cluster. It Talks Back!

Workshop and panel

Haggai Zohar (TeraSky) runs Company Brain with Fabric and Claude, connecting Claude to a Microsoft Fabric semantic layer over the Model Context Protocol so business users can ask questions without writing DAX or SQL. A panel with Adaya Tal (ReasonLabs) and Einat Borohovich (Rambam Health Care Campus), moderated by Sharone Revah Zitzman, closes on where data and AI go next.

Why a Conf42 viewer should go

If you watched Conf42 Large Language Models 2026 and wanted the follow-up conversation in person, this is it, with a heavier dose of storage and pipelines than most LLM days. Bring the migration war story you never got to tell; someone from the ClickHouse talk will want to hear it.

Register

The day starts at 09:00 at the Microsoft Reactor in Midtown Tel Aviv. Tickets are free and handled through in10t, linked from the LLMday Tel Aviv page, together with the full agenda. Seats are approved by the organisers, so apply early.

entry.title: LLMday Hamburg is about agents that have to ship, not demo
entry.summary: LLMday Hamburg, November 18 at House of AI - 15 talks from justtrack, vCluster Labs, ScyllaDB, DKB Code Factory and more. CONF42 = 42% off.
entry.content:
LLMday Hamburg runs on November 18, 2026, at House of AI, with fifteen talks on one track about getting agents and models through production instead of through a demo. Speakers come from justtrack, vCluster Labs, ScyllaDB, DKB Code Factory, OMR Reviews, HeyBreez AI, Adjoe and moebel.de, and the code CONF42 gets Conf42 readers 42% off the ticket.

The keynote is honest about what broke

Gabriel Awad (justtrack GmbH) opens with Design, Product, Engineering: What Our AI-Driven Design Workflow Fixed and What It Broke. justtrack rebuilt its design workflow as scoped agent skills (requirements, research, design, critique, pre-handoff check), and a feature now goes from ticket to clickable prototype in a day. The title promises the other half too, which is the part worth the train ticket.

Testing is the running theme

A surprising share of the day is about knowing whether the thing works.

  • Jan Kleine-Klatte (MoinMeister), Testing AI Agents Like Self-Driving Cars, brings nearly a decade of scenario-based testing and safety assurance from autonomous driving to agents.
  • Ebrahim Mirsafian (Lavan Labs), Testing Voice When Your Coding Agent Can't Hear. They build a voice co-worker with Claude Code, and the coding agent cannot tell whether the voice still works. Somebody has to listen.
  • Miroslav Dzunic (DKB Code Factory), Build Your Own Agentic Factory: Agents Still Need a Definition of Done. Fifteen years of hearing "done" from humans, now from agents.
  • Izabel Cvetkovic (OMR Reviews), Hallucination Gating for multi-agentic systems, on a grounding gate that stops a model from inventing a pricing tier the retrieved documents never mention.

Platforms, serving and memory

Piotr Zaniewski (vCluster Labs) argues in Your Platform Already Has AI Users that MCP servers, RAG services and agents already hit your platform APIs and need their own identity, context budget and guardrails. Philip Laine (Kvick) covers It's Time to Serve AI Models: 20-minute cold starts, OOMing nodes and restarting downloads, solved level by level. Attila Toth (ScyllaDB) explains the infrastructure behind "For You" feeds at companies like Tripadvisor and Medium, and Ivan Vokhmin (moebel.de) walks From RAG to memory decay, including how to retire stale context in a vector store.

The rest of the bill covers voice agents in operations (Faris Qatawneh, HeyBreez AI), a company brain (Shekhar Khandelwal, Adjoe), indirect prompt injection (Kristaps Pluto), who owns the harness (Lior Oren), an agent-built code foundry (Marcel Koert, MeloMar-IT) and spec-driven agentic development (Pedro Treuer, Netlight Consulting).

Why a Conf42 viewer should go

It overlaps neatly with Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026: the people building the platform and the people building the agents are in the same room, arguing about who gets paged. Harness sponsors the day alongside House of AI.

Register

Doors open at 09:00. Get a ticket on Luma and enter CONF42 at checkout for 42% off. The full schedule is on the LLMday Hamburg page.

entry.title: Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026: when agents become platform users
entry.summary: The Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 roundup - 26 talks on agents as platform users, delegated authority, GenAI as a platform primitive and real-time data.
entry.content:
Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 went out on November 5 with 26 talks, and the question running through most of them was new: what does a platform owe its users when some of those users are AI agents? Speakers from Harness, AWS, PayPal, Coinbase, Walmart, T-Mobile, Electronic Arts and a long list of smaller teams answered from very different angles, but they kept landing on the same ideas. Context has to be explicit, authority has to be scoped, and "done" has to be decided by code you own.

Not everything was about AI. The data, mobile and migration talks were a good reminder that the platform team's day job still includes Kafka, latency budgets and getting a legacy system off life support without downtime.

Agents are now a class of platform user

The keynote from Jimmy Caputo of Harness set the frame: platforms built for humans assume someone knows the tribal knowledge, spots noisy tests and watches deploys. Agents need that made explicit through a single context layer, deterministic pipelines they call instead of improvise, central policy and observability that feeds back into all three.

Yedidya Schwartz of Quicklizard brought the field report. His first ticket-to-PR pipeline went green on GitHub after the model quietly skipped three phases; his crash test across six durable engines showed that a thin controller, not the engine, stopped him paying twice for model calls. Erik Hanchett of AWS toured always-on "Claws", agents with memory, schedules and chat access, along with their rough edges.

Two talks looked at what happens after the code arrives faster. Lucas Mateus Mazei Sobrinho of MEMED S.A. treated AI as a stress test for the delivery system, where environments, reviews and approvals become the new queue. Shem Magnezi of Lemonade framed running side projects with AI as platform engineering at a team size of one: the hard part is operating what you built without becoming its permanent support team.

Authority, not just permissions

If one idea will outlive the event, it's the split between being able to do something and being allowed to decide it. Ruby Agarwal of Avaya walked a 2:14am incident where an agent is 96% sure a deploy caused it, and showed why the rollback still needs scoped, expiring authority, an independent check and verification of the customer outcome. Cynthia Akiotu of Accenture followed a poisoned refund policy through an agent and showed the system holding even when the model was fooled, because the export needed an authorization check the prompt couldn't grant.

The guardrail talks were refreshingly concrete. Sumeet L. Ram of PayPal described an MCP server used by more than 150 product teams across 200 markets, where the hard design problem was what the platform refuses to do. Niharika P Pujari of McGraw Hill compared prompting against architecture-level guardrails (Storybook, Playwright, axe-core, CI checks) for AI-generated frontends. Madhu Chenna of Electronic Arts presented a conceptual self-healing ops framework with confidence gates deciding when an agent may act. Leanid Piliptsevich of EPAM went lower: MazeWall, an experimental toolkit that lets JVM apps sandbox their own components with seccomp and Landlock.

GenAI as a platform primitive

Several talks treated models as infrastructure with tenants, budgets and SLOs. Brindal Patel of Coinbase, speaking from independent work, designed a GenAI gateway that holds token budgets like card payments, caches only after four safety checks and fails over only to models that passed your evals. Sergey Pronin of Solanica covered Model-as-a-Service on Kubernetes with KServe, vLLM and per-model quotas.

Scarlett Attensil of LaunchDarkly ran the event's tidiest experiment: packing five criteria into one LLM judge call cut cost by 46% with no measurable accuracy change, while 40 criteria cost about six points. Attila Toth of ScyllaDB explained the feature stores behind For You feeds, from P99 tail-latency maths to query-first data models.

Operating models and the metrics that prove them

Jeleel Muibi of HybridOps argued that Terraform and Ansible are tools, and the architecture is the layer that decides authority, completion and recovery, demoed as a preflight that refuses a shared network in a dev environment. Amith Reddy Ravuru of Reltio, an SAP company, proposed journey-based platform SLOs such as time to first environment and self-service completion rate. Eleftheria Batsou of UptimeRobot pointed at the gap in most golden paths: monitoring still gets set up by hand, later, if anyone remembers.

On the reliability side, Saikrishna Ala of Bath and Body Works shared a playbook for zero-downtime migrations built on dual writes, bidirectional sync and CDC, and Mohan Kumar Dalai of GE Vernova took platform thinking into power plants, where AI maintenance lives or dies on context and operator trust.

Real-time data platforms

The data track was full of hard constraints. Egor Kolovertnykh of BetBoom built an in-house Dota 2 draft feed from Game State Integration and reported conversion rising from 8.4% to 31.2%. Sujan Challa of Samsung Electronics America treated latency budgets as architecture in real-time bidding. Nidhin Jose of Walmart covered event-driven retail supply chains with Kafka, CQRS and sagas, and Vincenzo Santonastaso of IBM showed Debezium Platform turning CDC pipelines into self-service for multiple teams.

Mobile apps are platforms too

Two talks moved platform engineering inside a single binary. RanjithKumar Ragavan of T-Mobile explained how five autonomous teams ship into the T-Life app, used by 53 million active users, through versioned contracts and independent build pipelines. Denis Galkin of Robofinance turned scattered debug menus into a plugin-based Dev Mode framework owned like an internal product.

Thanks to the sponsors

Harness was the diamond sponsor, with SREday as gold sponsor and HockeyStick as podcast partner, alongside media partners including Manning and Packt.

Every talk is on the Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 page and in the YouTube playlist. Next in the series is Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, where several of these threads (evals, rollbacks, agents in production) continue from the model side.

entry.title: What an engineering platform owes its AI agents
entry.summary: Jimmy Caputo of Harness at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on the context layer, tools, guardrails and observability agents need to ship safely.
entry.content:
Most delivery platforms quietly assume a human is in the loop: someone who knows which test failures are noise, which directory not to touch, and when a deploy looks off. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, Jimmy Caputo, Senior Director of Product Management at Harness, asked what happens to those assumptions once agents write the code, run the tests and open the pull requests. His answer is a platform that hands agents four things: context, tools, guardrails and observability.

It's a compact, opinionated talk from a vendor, and it says so near the end, when Jimmy maps the ideas onto Harness. The first four-fifths stand on their own as a design checklist for any platform team.

The tribal knowledge has to move out of people's heads

Jimmy's starting point is scale. One agent per developer is manageable. Fleets of agents running in their own sandboxes, around the clock, turn code review into the bottleneck and make relying on someone to notice an unreliable control. Mistakes have to be caught and remediated automatically.

The first thing agents lack is context. Ownership (who to ask, who approves), architecture and dependencies beyond the current repo, coding standards and the definition of done, what is deployed where, whether an incident is in progress, which past changes caused trouble, and the actual intent of the task. If a human developer would have to gather that from ten systems or ten people, an agent won't reconstruct it reliably.

One context layer beats ten lookups per task

The sharpest argument is about cost. Without a single layer that brokers all this information, every agent session rebuilds the map from scratch: query the observability tool, work out what a service is called there, map it to the repo and the pipeline. It might manage, but it burns tokens and time on every start.

Jimmy's alternative is a platform that syncs with source systems in near real time, builds a knowledge graph of the system and the organisation once, and gives agents that graph as their primary context, with permission to go to the source system when something is missing or stale.

Agents shouldn't invent the SDLC on every task

The second pillar is tools that cover the whole life cycle, from reading and editing code to building, testing, deploying and checking health. The point isn't more tools; it's fewer, higher-level ones. If an agent stitches its own path from commit to production each time, steps get skipped or reordered, work gets duplicated, and occasionally something reaches production through a path nobody designed.

His fix is deterministic pipelines on an orchestration platform that agents call, so repeatability comes from the pipeline, not from the agent remembering the process.

Policy in one place, not in a thousand repos

The third pillar is guardrails: scoped access to data and tools, limits on what an agent may change on its own, and human approval where it matters. Jimmy's warning is about sprawl. You can encode rules as skills and conventions per repo or per IDE, but in a large organisation that becomes hundreds of copies of the same policy, some stale, some missing, with no way for the platform team to see what is enforced where. A central policy engine that every agent and tool connects to lets you define rules once.

Observability closes the loop

The fourth piece is observability that is designed in rather than bolted on: what the agent did, what it changed, why, and what happened next, including rollbacks and outages. Those signals should feed back into the other three pillars. Did the agent fail for lack of context, lack of a tool to check its work, or a missing guardrail that should have forced a human approval?

He adds a practical list for anything agents call: consistent APIs or MCP tools, actionable errors, machine-readable docs, published rate limits so agents back off instead of guessing, safe retries, and clear versioning and deprecation notices. None of it is exotic. All of it is the difference between an agent that recovers on its own and one that hammers an endpoint.

Autonomy is a dial

Jimmy's closing advice is the most reusable part: treat autonomy as a spectrum from suggestions to agents acting within guardrails, start at the level you are comfortable with, and pick one workflow or repository as the test bed. Build the context layer, tools and guardrails there, watch the outcomes, fill the gaps, then expand to other teams.

Who should watch

Platform teams being asked to support agents without a clear brief, and engineering leaders deciding how much autonomy to grant. If you want benchmarks or a live demo, this isn't it; it's a concise architecture talk with a product section at the end.

Related talks from other Conf42 events take the guardrail theme further: Gate the Action, Not the Alert by Artemis Leonardou at DevSecOps 2026, Your Agent Is Confidently Wrong by Girish Konda at Feature Flags 2026, and I Don't Trust AI Agents (And Neither Should You) by Morgan Willis at AI Agents 2026.

From Harness

In the talk, Jimmy describes how Harness covers these pillars: a knowledge graph built from first-party data (the code Harness manages and the build and deployment pipelines that run on it) plus connections to third-party systems; an orchestration engine whose pipelines agents can execute, with optional human approval steps or agent steps inside them; a policy engine that lets central teams restrict what developer teams can do; and observability over what the system is orchestrating. The platform lets each team choose how much autonomy agents get.

entry.title: Terraform and Ansible are tools; the operating model is the architecture
entry.summary: Jeleel Muibi of HybridOps at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on authority, preflight checks and run records that sit above Terraform and Ansible.
entry.content:
Every step in the pipeline went green, and the traffic still didn't move. That is the scene Jeleel Muibi, infrastructure and automation engineer and maintainer of the open-source HybridOps project, opens with at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026. His claim: Terraform provisions, Ansible configures and a pipeline sequences, but none of them decides whether a change should run or what "done" means. That decision layer is the architecture.

Three passes and a no

The opening slide is worth pausing on. Infrastructure is provisioned, configuration is applied, the health check passes, and the requested outcome still fails because something outside the pipeline wasn't ready. Each tool did its job. What was missing was a model of how the tools' outputs connect to the result anyone actually asked for.

Jeleel frames the gap with six boundaries, which he ties to the CNCF platform engineering maturity model: intent, authority, permission, readiness, completion and continuity. Tools live inside those boundaries. The operating model draws them.

Authority comes from outside the tool

The most practical idea is "authority is a scoped fact". In his example, a blueprint deploys a platform VM that must get its IP address from an IPAM, NetBox in the demo. Before any step runs, a preflight checks that the authoritative source is reachable and can answer. If it can't, the whole run stops with a clear failure instead of half-provisioning a VM that will later fight another one for an address.

Notice that the tool underneath doesn't matter. The VM could be built by Terraform, Pulumi, Ansible or a PowerShell script. The decision about whether it may be built belongs to the layer above.

Fail fast at the boundary that owns the decision

The demo, run in VS Code against the HybridOps repository, walks through validate, plan and preflight for an on-prem foundation on Proxmox SDN. The fun moment is a refusal. Jeleel runs preflight for a shared network foundation in a dev environment, and the policy rejects it: shared foundations belong in the shared environment, and dev should consume them, not create its own copy. Run the same Terraform module on its own and it would have happily deployed to dev, setting up a VLAN or IP conflict for later.

Because the network step was blocked, the inventory and platform steps were deferred and nothing external changed. Terraform's own plan stage catches conflicts within Terraform; this check catches conflicts between tools and environments, which is where multi-tool platforms tend to bleed.

A refusal should tell you what to do next

The last section is about evidence. A run should leave a reviewable chain, not a folder of terraform.log, ansible.log and Packer output that someone has to correlate at 2am. A good refusal names the blueprint, the policy that blocked it, the selected environment, the deferred steps, the owner of the decision and the path to fix it.

His starting advice for teams with a pile of hand-triggered pipelines is pleasantly unglamorous: pick one risky end-to-end workflow, name its outcome, assign authority, move the checks before execution, define completion with a signal the service owns, keep the record, then repeat. Keep the tools, design the architecture around them, and swapping a tool later stops being a migration project.

Who should watch

Platform and infrastructure engineers who own Terraform and Ansible estates across on-prem and cloud, especially anyone who has explained a green pipeline in a post-incident review. Be aware that the demo uses HybridOps, Jeleel's own MIT-licensed project, as the worked example; the pattern applies without it. The talk runs long and the delivery is conversational, so the slides on boundaries and refusals carry most of the value.

entry.title: Power plant AI maintenance runs on context, not more sensor data
entry.summary: Mohan Kumar Dalai of GE Vernova at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on AI maintenance platforms that read context, cut alarm floods and keep humans in charge.
entry.content:
A power plant already has more data than it can read. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, Mohan Kumar Dalai, staff software engineer at GE Vernova, argued that the job of AI in maintenance is to turn that pile into decisions an engineer will trust, and that the hard part is context and adoption, not the model.

It's a short, clear talk aimed at people who build platforms for operational technology rather than at data scientists. If your users wear hard hats, it's worth the time.

Failures are slow; schedules are blind

Mohan starts with the two maintenance styles every plant knows. Reactive maintenance fixes things after they break. Time-based maintenance inspects or replaces on a calendar. Both have value, and both miss the point that most failures develop gradually. A turbine bearing doesn't die overnight, and a transformer fault starts inside long before anyone can see it.

So the question shifts from when the asset was last serviced to what the equipment is saying right now. That is condition-based thinking, and it's the foundation the rest of the talk builds on.

A vibration spike is a question, not an answer

The sharpest section is about context. A rise in vibration on a rotating asset could mean degradation. It could also mean a recent startup, a load change, a hot afternoon or a drifting sensor. Without context, all of those look the same on a chart.

Mohan's case for AI here is specific: models are useful because they evaluate relationships between operating conditions instead of single data points. Instead of fixed thresholds, the system learns what normal looks like for each machine at each load. The payoff he stressed is alert quality. Fewer false alarms means operators keep listening, which anyone who has muted a noisy Slack channel will recognise.

He walks the same idea across three asset families:

  • Rotating machinery (turbines, generators, pumps, bearings): earlier detection of lubrication problems, misalignment, imbalance and wear.
  • Boilers and heat systems: spotting drift in relationships, like fuel use rising without more output, that never crosses a classic alarm threshold.
  • Transformers: dissolved gas analysis, where trend direction and persistence matter more than any single reading, and explainability is non-negotiable.

AI should organise alarms, not hide them

Control rooms rarely lack information; they drown in it. During abnormal events operators can get hundreds of notifications. Mohan's line is that AI's job is to group related alarms, point at likely causes and add context, while decision authority stays with the human operator.

That ties into the platform half of the talk. He lists the reasons AI maintenance projects stall, and none of them is the algorithm: data quality, integration with legacy systems, explainability requirements and cybersecurity. His five-step path is plain on purpose: define the problem, build reliable data foundations, develop and validate models, deploy under governance with continuous feedback, and judge the result by operational outcomes rather than by how many graphs it produces.

Trust is the real deployment target

The adoption advice reads like it came from someone who has watched a good model get ignored. Show the signal, the reasoning and the evidence. Fit existing workflows instead of adding steps. Let users challenge a recommendation. Mohan frames the goal as partnership, not dependency, and closes with the claim that AI strengthens maintenance engineering rather than replacing it.

The forward-looking part covers digital twins, inspection robots for hazardous areas and fleet analytics, where a lesson learned at one plant reaches dozens of others.

Who should watch

Platform and reliability engineers working with industrial or energy customers, and anyone building an internal AI service that operators must trust before they act on it. If you want model architectures, benchmarks or code, this isn't that talk; it's an overview of the operating model around the models.

entry.title: Replace the system the business runs on without a big-bang weekend
entry.summary: Saikrishna Ala (Bath and Body Works) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on dual-write, bidirectional sync and CDC as reusable migration capability.
entry.content:
A big-bang cutover concentrates every risk of a migration into one weekend and gives you exactly one shot. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, Saikrishna Ala, Senior Applications Developer at Bath and Body Works who leads data integration and platform modernisation, laid out a practitioner playbook for replacing systems the business uses every hour: three patterns, a readiness check before the flip, and an argument for building all of it once as platform capability.

His running example is Bath and Body Works' order management migration from Radial to Manhattan Active Omni, with 100% of order traffic and zero tolerance for downtime.

Why the rehearsed weekend still fails

Big-bang plans look manageable on paper: one weekend, a runbook, a rollback plan. What they hide, in Saikrishna's list: data drift your test environment never reveals, no validation on real (messy, voluminous) traffic, a rollback that becomes very hard once records have landed in the new system, and a blast radius that hits every user and integration at once.

Pattern one: dual-write and parallel run

Every write goes to both legacy and new systems; legacy stays the source of truth and serves reads; an automated reconciliation layer compares the two. He breaks it into five phases: shadow (new system takes writes, legacy serves all reads), compare (fix every divergence, which can take weeks, so don't skip it), canary reads (a small slice of reads from the new system), flip (new becomes source of truth, legacy stays as fallback), and retire. The discipline: don't move from compare to canary until divergence is at or near zero. Decide up front your reconciliation latency target, how divergences reach engineers, and how fast you can roll reads back.

Pattern two: bidirectional sync for long coexistence

When teams will sit on different systems for months while users migrate in waves, a sync layer keeps both alive and consistent. His four non-negotiables:

  • Resolve conflicts deterministically: per-field ownership, or last-write-wins with timestamps. Figuring it out at runtime is not a strategy.
  • Prevent echo loops: every change carries an origin tag, and the sync layer never sends a change back where it came from.
  • Make every write idempotent: replays will happen, so use upserts everywhere.
  • Preserve ordering per entity: out-of-order applies leave data inconsistent.

Pattern three: CDC from the transaction log

Change data capture reads the legacy database's transaction log, with no schema changes or application instrumentation and no batch queries against the legacy app. Events go to a durable, replayable stream, and the new platform, search index and analytics consume it independently. The abstract cites Forrester data that event-driven approaches can cut data latency from hours to milliseconds; in the talk he puts most CDC workloads at milliseconds to seconds, versus hours of lag for batch ETL. Three operating rules: take a full snapshot before streaming increments, handle schema changes as versioned events, and monitor consumer lag end to end. Lag, he says, is the migration's heartbeat.

Most real migrations combine them: CDC for the data layer, dual-write or bidirectional sync for the application layer. Dual-write proves the new system on production traffic but needs an application change; sync suits long coexistence at the cost of the sync layer itself; CDC suits high-volume movement when you can't touch the legacy app, with lag and schema drift as the risks.

Score readiness, then pick a date

Before cutover, score five dimensions: latency (how fresh is data on both sides), reliability (does sync survive failure and replay, chaos-tested before the flip), bidirectionality (changes flow both ways without loops or corruption), scalability (load-tested at peak, not average) and migration safety (verified rollback, no-go checklist, step-by-step plan). If you can't score all five with confidence, you're not ready. Set the date when you can, not before.

The organisational point closes the talk. When every migration team builds its own sync and reconciliation, safety guarantees are inconsistent and every cutover is a heroic weekend. Built once as platform primitives, cutovers become routine engineering, and the investment pays back from the second migration on.

Who should watch

Platform and data teams facing an OMS, CRM, claims or similar replacement, and anyone who needs to argue internally for funding migration tooling instead of another heroic weekend. It's a patterns-and-checklists talk rather than a detailed account of the Bath and Body Works migration itself.

entry.title: Gate every automated IT fix on a confidence score
entry.summary: Madhu Chenna (Electronic Arts) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 presents ADOF, a reference architecture for self-healing IT ops with confidence-gated AI agents.
entry.content:
The disk that fills up slowly is the classic IT ticket nobody needed to file: the signal was there for days. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, Madhu Chenna, Senior Manager at Electronic Arts, presented the Autonomous Digital Operations Framework (ADOF), a conceptual reference architecture for moving enterprise IT support from firefighting to governed automation, built around one design decision: every automated action has to earn a confidence score before it runs.

Honest scope, which Madhu states clearly himself: ADOF is a blueprint, not a product and not a case study. Its numbers are illustrative targets proposed for future validation.

Silos make IT reactive

Monitoring, endpoint management and ITSM tools rarely talk to each other. An alert shows up in one, a spike of slowness tickets in another, and a human connects the dots under pressure. Madhu cites industry data, which he says his own experience validates, that up to 40% of Level-1 requests come from issues existing telemetry could have anticipated. Even repeatable, low-risk fixes such as clearing a temp folder or restarting a known flaky service still wait on a person.

Unify, retrieve, specialise

ADOF's foundation is signal unification: endpoint telemetry (CPU, memory, disk, crashes, patch state), ITSM context (incident history, SLAs, change records) and asset metadata (owner, criticality, lifecycle) in one queryable stream. His example: a specific laptop model used by developers has frequent GPU driver crashes. One tool sees isolated crashes; correlated with who uses those laptops and a rise in slowness tickets from the same people, it becomes a systemic issue flagged before it hits a critical team.

On top sits RAG over runbooks, KB articles, postmortems and vendor docs, continuously ingested so agents retrieve the current fix rather than last year's. Then six specialised agents instead of one general one: incident prediction, asset health (for example predicting laptop battery failure), auto-remediation, procurement intelligence (order the replacement before the old machine dies), user experience (tie slow app loads to backend events), and a compliance and audit agent that checks every proposed action against policy.

The confidence gate

Before acting, an agent computes a composite score from three dimensions. Enterprise health: is the environment already unstable, so the blast radius of any change is bigger? Business impact: is this an internal wiki or a production game authentication server? Automation confidence: how often has this exact action pattern worked before?

Example thresholds: above 85%, execute autonomously. Between 60% and 85%, create a ticket with the probable root cause and a recommended fix behind a one-click approval. Below 60%, full manual review. Madhu's argument is that this middle band, assisted recommendation, is where human trust gets built.

Every outcome feeds back. Successful fixes raise the confidence for that pattern; human overrides become labelled training signals; drift detection notices when a fix that used to work starts failing. Autonomy grows through a five-level maturity model: observe, recommend, assisted execution (the gate switches on), supervised autonomy with humans reviewing exceptions, and finally full autonomy with continuous policy validation and audit logging.

What to take back on Monday

His four patterns are usable without adopting the whole framework: unify signals before automating anything; gate on a confidence score instead of static rules; start with one specialised agent domain, such as asset health; and build outcome capture first, since a system that doesn't record whether its fixes worked can't improve.

Who should watch

IT operations and internal platform leaders sketching an AIOps roadmap who want a vocabulary for governed autonomy. If you want production results and a war story, this isn't that; it's an architecture proposal, presented as one.

entry.title: Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026 - the prompt is the smallest part
entry.summary: Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026 in review, 18 talks on context contracts, prompt drift, injection defence, regulated workflows and agents in production.
entry.content:
Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026 ran on October 29, 2026 with 18 talks, and almost none of them were about wording. The consensus across the day: a prompt is one input to a system, and the reliability lives in the contracts, context budgets, traces and rollout controls around it. Engineers from Adobe, Meta, eBay, Harness, Tech Mahindra and a handful of startups showed what that looks like when real users, regulators and attackers show up.

Context is an engineering artefact with a budget

Emerson Braun (Plan A Technologies) set the tone with "Prompting Is Not the System". He walks a realistic agent workflow and lists where it breaks: stale context, instructions that conflict with tool permissions, retries that repeat side effects, and prompts that grow until nobody knows what the agent may do. His fix treats context as a versioned input contract and moves tool schemas, permissions and failure behaviour out of the prompt.

Nishant Kumar Thakur and Sonam Raj (Adobe) brought the numbers. Pre-loading MCP tool schemas burned 150K tokens before the model read the user's question, and tool selection was right only 42% of the time. Code Mode, which swaps the schema dump for typed API stubs the model reads like library code, took that to 22K tokens and 80% accuracy. Same tools, different presentation.

Ian Johnson (Parento) asked the organisational version in "Whose gate is it?": every team running coding agents has a charter, a harness and a factory, and almost nobody has drawn the lines between them. He walks one rule down the rungs where a gate can sit and separates two boundaries, what a thing governs and who gets paged when it is wrong. Kevin Brown (Cloud World Model) pointed at a different gap: an agent can write Terraform but cannot feel what it breaks, so he simulates a proposed infrastructure change before merge and labels every number as modelled, estimated or a known gap.

Prompts behave like software, so test them like software

Sachin Gupta (eBay) proposed prompt contracts: required fields, banned claims, citation rules and token ceilings, enforced with JSON schema validation plus golden and fuzz tests in CI. His demo is a real regression caused by a harmless-looking prompt tweak, caught before users noticed. Emmanuela Opurum (SoftNet Technologies) covered the same ground from the workflow side: prompt drift, weak evaluation and over-reliance on manual experimentation as the usual ways prompt-driven apps go wrong.

You can't fix what you can't see fail

Observability got its own track. Krishna Chaitanya Balusu (Meta) authored the plan operation for agent planning spans in the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions, and showed how a first-class planning span lets you tell a planning failure from a tool failure, with a demo that catches a fault a final-answer check misses. Indika Wimalasuriya (Virtusa) traced a request through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore end to end in Datadog, correlating LLM signals with ordinary APM, logs and infrastructure.

Diamond sponsor Harness closed the loop. Nicolas Zelaya showed offline evals going green on a cheaper model, then a 20% canary in which every trace span stayed green while users got wrong answers and the cost per finished session went up. Rollback was a traffic edit, and the failed sessions became new eval cases.

One guardrail is a demo, two are a design

Manvitha Potluri (24x7 Systems) tested LLM guardrails on AWS Bedrock against 390 attack prompts in 15 categories: direct and indirect injection, role-play jailbreaks, encoding tricks, and attempts to fire destructive tool calls. Her case is for dual detection, a managed guardrail plus an independent second check, and for catching harmful actions before they execute rather than grading text after the fact. She also spends time on the cost of blocking too much, which security talks usually skip.

When the output has to survive an auditor

Three talks took prompting into regulated work. Mohit Upadhyay (Tech Mahindra) built a permitting platform that automates NEPA Categorical Exclusion determinations for historically sensitive sites, combining RAG, computer vision and geospatial data while keeping traceability and human oversight. Vraj Patel (Apptronik) used bounded, human-supervised agents for safety assurance in physical AI, with the MBSE model as the single source of truth across ISO 26262, ISO 21448, UL 4600 and ASPICE. Pratik Patel (Hexaware Technologies) applied the same discipline to anti-money-laundering workflows: grounded data products, factual extraction kept apart from interpretive reasoning, and no unsupported conclusions in a compliance decision.

From pilot to product, with retrieval doing the heavy lifting

Ahmed Gaber and Ahmed Morsi (Nowlun) took a customer-facing agent to production and found the single large system prompt broke under real traffic; intent detection, grounded tool calls and clear handoff rules to humans made it predictable, and real escalations became the eval set. Aleem Khan went the other way from the API: a real-time news pipeline that classifies around 70 types of bias started on frontier-model prompts, then used their outputs plus human review to train an in-house model that replaced most of the calls. LaShawnda Rodgers (RGLC) argued that a product starts long before the first prompt and showed her repeatable process for building and launching real apps.

On retrieval, Santosh Muthyala (Meta) personalised enterprise analytics RAG with a user profile store and five specialised indices, so a senior data engineer gets SQL-first answers and a product manager gets KPIs. Ravi Ray compared roughly 25 RAG implementations on a five-axis framework and made the case for ACL-aware retrieval, provenance and time-aware evaluation.

Sponsors and where to watch

Thanks to Harness and LLMday, the Diamond sponsors, and to the Prompt Engineering Conference at Gold. Every talk is on the event page and in the YouTube playlist.

The series is back with Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2027. If this year is a guide, the talks will be even less about prompts.

entry.title: Platform SLOs should stop the clock at ready, not provisioned
entry.summary: Amith Reddy Ravuru (Reltio) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on journey SLOs that measure a developer's path from request to production-ready.
entry.content:
Every platform SLO can be green while a developer spends four days getting a working environment. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, Amith Reddy Ravuru, Staff Platform Architect at Reltio, an SAP company, made the case for journey SLOs: measure the developer's trip from asking for something to putting real traffic on it, because the waiting lives between your services, where no dashboard looks.

He says the examples come from things his team got wrong and then fixed, and the numbers in the talk are illustrative. The method is the point.

The watermelon week

Amith's opening story: on Monday a developer asks for a new tenant environment, the textbook golden-path request. The platform dashboard has a great week: 99.95% API availability, 180 ms p99, tiny error rate. The developer's week: a quota ticket Monday, a chat thread about network access Tuesday, a policy exception from another team Wednesday, first deploy works Friday.

Lay the request out on a timeline and the services did perhaps 40 minutes of work. The rest was queues, approvals and manual fixes, none of which has an SLO or an owner. IT service management folks call it the watermelon effect: green outside, red inside. Operational SLOs stop at the service boundary; developers live in the gaps.

Five stages and one journey ID

His journey has five stages: requested, provisioned, usable (log in and do a first real deploy, not just get a 200), policy-compliant (no open exceptions), and operationally ready (monitoring set up, alerts routed to a real on-call). Many dashboards declare victory at provisioned. Amith's rule is that provisioned is the platform's milestone and first deploy is the developer's.

A journey SLI is good journeys over total journeys in a window, where good means reaching ready in time without rework. It spans five services and maybe three teams, so someone has to own the whole path, and on a platform team that's you. The glue is a journey ID minted at request time and carried everywhere as a tag or label, so workflow events, pipeline events, tickets, chat and policy checks can be joined into one record per journey.

Six indicators in three honest pairs

Each pair keeps the other from being gamed, an idea he credits to the SPACE paper:

  • Faster: time to first environment (request to first successful deploy) and time to operational readiness (until the last readiness check passes; record which check was last, and for his team it was usually alert routing).
  • Safer: failed-workflow recovery time, split by cause (quota, permissions, policy, cloud API, product bug), and rework rate, any redo within 14 days after handoff.
  • Easier: self-service completion rate, where one manual runbook step or side-channel approval disqualifies the journey, and support dependency, help requests per 100 journeys. A nice trick: have the platform channel's bot ask which journey a question is about.

Data is mostly already there. Add one pulse question when a journey ends, rated one to five, because telemetry and people each miss things: a step can be fast and confusing, or slow and so familiar nobody complains anymore.

His multi-cloud tenant example adds orchestration metrics: planning accuracy on the bill of materials, hand-off wait to each component team, and which component lands last on the critical path. One example record shows a flow efficiency of 18%, so the tenant spent most of its life sitting in queues.

Six ways to get it wrong

The anti-patterns are worth the watch alone. Reporting averages (four two-hour journeys and one four-day one average to 21 hours, hiding the person who lost a week). Stopping the clock at provisioned. Pushing one indicator alone. Hiding a human step behind a portal button. Setting targets before a baseline. And ranking component teams on a league table, which makes people manage the number instead of the journey.

His rollout plan fits in a month: define done for one painful journey, instrument it with a journey ID, watch real journeys for a baseline, then set targets and a journey error budget.

Who should watch

Platform product owners asked to prove the golden path works, and SREs who want to point SLO thinking at internal users. It pairs well with any DORA or SPACE reading you've already done.

entry.title: Your agent's evals passed. The canary is where it actually gets tested
entry.summary: Nicolas Zelaya of Harness at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026 on offline evals, versioned AI configs and agent canaries as one release loop.
entry.content:
A green eval suite tells you a prompt change is ready for traffic, not that it is better. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026, Nicolas Zelaya, Director of Product Management at Harness, walked one agent change from offline evals through a 20% canary and back, and showed the moment where every trace span was green while the agent still failed its users.

It is a vendor talk and says so: the tooling on screen is Harness Feature Management & Experimentation (FME) with its AI evals and AI configs. The loop he draws, though, is one any team shipping agents has to build somehow.

The question is "did it work", asked four ways

Zelaya opens with four questions about the last change you shipped to your agent: how did you know it was better, how did you know it was safe, did it move the business the way you expected, and how fast could you iterate if it didn't. He frames the problem with a 2026 survey he cites in which 74% of enterprises had to roll back or shut down an agent rollout. Writing the agent is no longer the bottleneck. Releasing it safely, and knowing what it actually did, is.

His running example is the most common agent change there is: swap to a cheaper model. Usually the bill does go down. The catch is whether quality holds, and his line for it is worth pinning above the desk: cheaper on the test suite does not always map to cheaper in production.

Evals are the unit tests, and unit tests are not the release

In his framing, evals are the unit tests of your agent: a dataset of golden cases plus the metrics you score against. Harness ships more than fifty built-in metrics, from deterministic checks and policy compliance to prompt-injection validation and LLM-as-a-judge rubrics. In the demo, a fintech-style agent answers "what is the fee on a late payment" under a set of rules; some tests fail, the prompt is iterated, the suite goes green.

Green here means the variation has earned traffic. That is all it means.

One versioned object for the prompt, the tools and the limits

The piece that makes the canary possible is what Harness calls an AI config: a single versioned object holding the system prompt, user prompt templates, tool access, policy checks and limits, with several variations you can assign traffic to. Your application still executes the agent; the config decides how it runs and for whom. The SDK picks the variation per user, sticky and consistent, while you set the split from the UI, the API or the MCP server.

Every run then sends traces and events back: task success, turns, latency, limit hits, proposed actions, tool use, plus a thumbs up or down at the end of a session. Each property can become a metric compared against the baseline.

Every span was green and four users got no answer

This is the part to watch. In the canary, every tool call succeeded. Nothing lit up on any dashboard. But four of the five test conversations asked about money coming in, and the tool returned money going out, until the token budget cut the run short. Task completion against the baseline dropped, and the cost per finished session came out higher, the opposite of what the cheaper model promised offline.

Rollback in this world is a traffic edit: move exposure off the candidate variation, no redeploy, and the change lands in the audit history. Then the production sessions that went wrong feed back into the eval dataset, a missing check gets added so the agent recognises when the data isn't there, and the same model with the same limits and tools goes back out to 20%. By the third wave, he showed the business outcome holding and the savings kept.

Who should watch

Anyone who owns an agent in production and has been treating a passing eval run as a release decision. If you already run feature flags for code, the talk is a useful map of how the same rollout discipline (percentage splits, baselines, guardrail metrics, instant rollback) carries over to prompts and model choices. His homework list for Monday is short and good: what does your eval not check, what is your canary slice, what is your baseline outcome, and what is your rollback.

entry.title: Monitoring belongs in the deploy, not in someone's memory
entry.summary: Eleftheria Batsou (UptimeRobot) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on creating monitors from the pipeline with a CLI, and what still needs a human.
entry.content:
Platform teams automated the repo template, the pipeline, the secrets, the infrastructure and the dashboards, and then left monitoring to a human with a web form, later, if anyone remembers. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, Eleftheria Batsou, Developer Advocate at UptimeRobot, gave a lightning talk on closing that gap by making monitor creation a deploy step from the command line.

Scope note: the examples use UptimeRobot's own open-source CLI, because that's what she works on. The argument, about where monitoring sits in the workflow, applies to any tool.

One root cause, three symptoms

Eleftheria names the failure modes precisely. No monitor at all, so the first alert is a customer support ticket. The wrong monitor: it checks the marketing homepage instead of the health endpoint, or pages someone who left last spring, and stays green while telling you nothing. And orphaned monitors for renamed or retired services, alerting on nothing or quietly checking a URL that now belongs to something else.

Every monitoring tool can hit an HTTP endpoint, so this isn't a tooling gap. Monitoring sits outside the golden path, so it runs on discipline rather than defaults, and discipline doesn't scale: 50 new services a year means 50 separate acts of remembering. Her fix is one default: build, test, deploy, register the monitor, confirm the service reports up. The pipeline already knows the service name, URL, owning team and environment, the exact fields someone would otherwise copy into a form.

Dry-run in the pull request

The CLI installs from npm, stores your key in the OS keychain locally, and reads it from an environment variable in CI. Creating a monitor is one command with type, name, URL, interval and timeout. Her favourite feature is --dry-run: it validates the request and prints the exact POST it would send, without credentials or network. That means a service's monitoring config can be checked in a PR the way you'd lint a Dockerfile. Leave out the timeout and it exits with code 2 and names the missing field.

Then the platform team gets opinionated. Template what's decided once: interval per tier, timeout, HTTP method, success codes, SSL and domain expiry reminders, tag conventions, alert-contact mapping. Take from service metadata what genuinely varies: name and environment, health endpoint, owning team, tier, a job's schedule. If you're copying the same value into every service, it belongs in the template.

The details that bite on the first run

This part is the most practical in the talk:

  • No upsert. The CLI retries reads but never POST, PATCH or DELETE. Call create on every deploy and you get a duplicate monitor every deploy. Look up first, create if missing, otherwise update; the name filter is a partial match, so compare exact names yourself and use something predictable like service plus environment.
  • Keys. Creating monitors needs the main API key. A read-only key gets a 403 and exit code 5.
  • Flags and plans. Interval and timeout are both required and everyone forgets timeout. The free plan's minimum interval is five minutes, so a template that hard-codes 30 seconds fails for every team.
  • HEAD by default. Without a method, HTTP monitors send HEAD, which some frameworks route differently from GET. Pass GET explicitly.

Exit codes are distinct (2 invalid input, 4 and 5 auth, 7 rate limit, 8 conflict) and errors arrive as JSON on stderr. Her policy: fail the deploy on config errors, since they mean shipping unmonitored, but don't block a release because a third-party API is briefly rate-limiting you. For cron jobs and queue workers with no URL, flip direction with a heartbeat monitor the job calls on completion; the CLI redacts that URL by default because it's effectively a secret.

Where a CLI is the wrong tool

Eleftheria is upfront about it. For whole-fleet desired state with drift detection, use a declarative tool. For AI agents investigating incidents, an MCP server beats shelling out. At 3am, a human in the dashboard wins. Whatever you choose, keep one source of truth per monitor; pipelines that create monitors people then edit by hand are a drift factory. And some monitoring can't be templated at all: which third-party services you depend on, journeys that cross services, who gets woken up, and response-time thresholds for a service with no traffic yet. Those stay human decisions, made consciously.

Who should watch

Platform teams with a golden path that stops at deploy. It's short, concrete and directly copyable, with CLI specifics you can skip if you use something else.
