entry.title: Better enterprise AI answers start before the prompt reaches the model
entry.summary: Ravi Ray at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026 on a vendor-neutral five-axis framework for enterprise RAG, from ingestion to governance.
entry.content:
Two assistants with the same model and nearly the same prompt answer a question about travel policy. One retrieves last year's policy, the other the current approved version. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026, Ravi Ray, a software engineering PMTS, used that example to argue that in enterprise AI the retrieved context often matters more than the prompt wording, and laid out a vendor-neutral five-axis framework for designing the retrieval layer.

The framework comes from a comparative look at roughly 25 implementations across academic research, open source frameworks and enterprise platforms. The aim wasn't to rank vendors but to find what changes when RAG leaves the prototype.

RAG is infrastructure now

A prototype is a few PDFs, some embeddings and useful answers, and Ravi calls that a good way to start. Production brings changing content, multiple repositories, permissions and users who expect the same answer every day. So treat RAG like databases, APIs and identity: reliable ingestion, predictable performance, clear ownership, monitoring. The question shifts from "can the model retrieve something relevant?" to whether the whole system retrieves the right evidence consistently, securely and at scale.

Five axes that affect each other

The axes are ingestion (parsing, normalising, chunking), indexing (dense, sparse or hybrid), retrieval composition (query rewriting, merging, re-ranking), grounding (tying answers to evidence) and governance (permissions, provenance, auditability). They aren't separate boxes: a great re-ranker can't restore a table the parser dropped, and accurate search is still unsafe if access controls are ignored.

Inspect what the parser actually produced

Ingestion is where many retrieval problems begin. A technical PDF loses a column heading during parsing, and later a search returns text that looks relevant but no longer means what the author wrote. No prompt tweak or vector database setting fixes that. His advice: look at the extracted content, chunk boundaries and metadata (author, last update, access, origin) before tuning retrieval, or you're optimising against damaged evidence.

On indexing, dense retrieval handles paraphrase, sparse retrieval like BM25 handles exact identifiers and product codes, which is why hybrid search plus a re-ranker is common in the systems he studied. Every extra stage costs latency and operational complexity, so measure end to end on real questions. The best pipeline is the simplest one that reliably meets the requirements.

Grounding and governance are architecture

Grounding means attribution to the specific chunk, faithfulness to that evidence, and visible confidence: if the policy documents don't describe an exception, the assistant says it couldn't verify one. A link to a hundred-page PDF is a decorative citation; a pointer to the right section is a useful one.

Governance is where research demos turn into hard enterprise projects. Enforce access control when candidates are selected, not just when results are displayed. Keep provenance from answer to chunk to source document and version. And evaluate with time in mind: an answer can be semantically correct and based on a pricing policy revised last month, which can do more harm than an obvious failure. Retrofitting any of these later is much harder.

Seven open problems

He lists the challenges still unsolved: grounding claims across long documents, ranking tables, diagrams, code and prose coherently, freshness through change data capture including deletions, evaluation that doesn't export confidential documents, multi-agent retrieval without duplicated or conflicting evidence, the latency and cost of extra passes, and evaluating under real enterprise conditions that public benchmarks don't capture. The gap between prototype and production, in his reading, is mostly operational, organisational and sometimes regulatory, not algorithmic.

His bigger shift is to design RAG as a knowledge system: source content as governed data with schemas, versions, permissions and change events, and the index as a derived representation, never the source of truth.

Four things to do on Monday

Audit ingestion by reading the extracted text behind real answers. Enforce access control at retrieval time and test with users who hold different permissions. Instrument provenance back to source and version. Build an evaluation set from real questions that includes outdated documents, exact identifiers, missing evidence and restricted content.

Who should watch

Architects and platform teams moving a RAG assistant from pilot to production, and prompt engineers who suspect their prompt isn't the problem. It's a framework talk without a demo or benchmark numbers, but the checklist is concrete enough to run against your own system.

entry.title: Model-as-a-service on Kubernetes is database-as-a-service again
entry.summary: Sergey Pronin (Solanica, OpenEverest) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on serving LLMs with KServe, vLLM, an AI gateway and per-key token limits.
entry.content:
If someone filed a ticket saying "we need to run LLMs on our cluster" with no further detail, Sergey Pronin built his talk for you. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, the founder of Solanica and maintainer of OpenEverest, a CNCF project for running databases on Kubernetes, walked through adding model-as-a-service to OpenEverest, and his recurring punchline is that platform engineers have solved this before: it's database-as-a-service with different nouns.

The talk is framed as a bar joke. The platform engineer wants reproducibility, the LLM wants a big GPU nobody else is using, Kubernetes wants everything to be an object with a reconciler. The rest is how each gets served.

Parameters times two

Why self-host at all? Sergey hears three reasons: data that can't leave (banks, healthcare, government, plenty of Europe), cost once token volume is steady and high, and GPUs that companies already bought and left idle.

Then the one piece of maths for the whole talk. A model is a folder of files full of weights, which he likens to a database's read-only data files. All of them must sit in GPU memory at two bytes each, so parameters times two is roughly gigabytes. A 4B model needs about 8 GB; a 70B Llama needs about 141 GB and won't fit even an 80 GB H100. And weights aren't the only tenant: the key-value cache holds every in-flight conversation, like a buffer pool. When it fills, requests queue. A model that fits isn't the same as a model that serves.

From one command to an operator

Day one is easy: vllm serve <model> on a GPU box gives you an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Day one on Kubernetes is a Deployment with nvidia.com/gpu: 1. Day two is the familiar mess: every restart re-downloads the weights, upgrades are manual, per-model flags live in someone's head, and the next team copies your YAML and changes three lines.

Sergey has seen this film. Ten years ago it was Postgres as a StatefulSet plus a pile of YAML, and the answer was operators. For models the operator is KServe: one LLM inference service object (which model, how many GPUs, how many replicas) and a reconciler that keeps a vLLM pod running on a GPU and rolls out changes.

A gateway, a key per app, a token budget

One model for one team isn't a platform. With four models you'd have four URLs, so an Envoy AI Gateway sits in front and routes by the model field in the request body; clients only change their base URL. Sergey compares it to PgBouncer or ProxySQL.

Then the questions every DBA has asked. A shared API key is a shared superuser password, so every app gets its own key, rotated or revoked without touching anyone else. Limits are in tokens rather than requests, because one request can be ten tokens or ten thousand. In his example each key gets 3,000 tokens an hour; the batch job that burns through its budget gets a too-many-requests error while the chat app carries on. Counters live in Redis or Valkey. And because every token is tagged with a key, asking who used all the GPUs becomes one Prometheus query instead of a meeting.

When it doesn't fit, split it; when it's busy, scale on the queue

On his 20 GB test cards, a 14B Qwen model dies with out-of-memory. No amount of YAML fixes physics. A model is also a stack of layers, so vLLM's pipeline parallelism spreads them across nodes, run by KServe with the Kubernetes LeaderWorkerSet project: one head pod serves the API, workers hold the rest, and every request visits each in turn, like sharding where every query hits every shard. The catch: the group lives and dies together, and two replicas means two whole groups.

For autoscaling, CPU is the wrong signal; models leave it idle. KServe's workload variant autoscaler scales on the KV-cache queue. And scaling up takes minutes rather than seconds, since a new pod pulls a multi-gigabyte image and then the weights, so keep weights on a cluster volume instead of fetching from Hugging Face, and keep a warm replica if you can afford it. Time to first token and requests waiting are the two health metrics he watches first.

Who should watch

Platform engineers who just inherited the LLM ticket, especially anyone who has run databases on Kubernetes. Sergey is a maintainer, and the last part shows how OpenEverest wraps all of this as just another instance next to Postgres and ClickHouse, but the architecture is open source building blocks you can assemble yourself.

entry.title: Put frontend standards in the platform, not in the prompt
entry.summary: Niharika P Pujari (McGraw Hill) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on guardrails for AI-generated frontends with design systems, Storybook, Playwright, axe-core and CI.
entry.content:
A generated dialog can look perfect in the browser and still lose keyboard focus the moment it closes. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, Niharika P Pujari, Lead Software Engineer at McGraw Hill working across frontend architecture, accessibility and software quality, argued that AI-generated frontend code shouldn't get its own, looser path: the standards we expect from humans should live in components, tests and CI gates that both humans and coding agents run into by default.

Her question is the right one for platform teams: how do you shape the environment so generated code lands closer to the standards in the first place, instead of reviewing it ever harder afterwards?

Three ways to ask a model for a form

Niharika compares three approaches, using accessibility as the running example.

  1. Generate first. Ask for a feature and review what comes back. It feels fast because progress is visible, but frontend quality is behavioural. A dialog may render and lose focus; a validation message may show but never be announced; a custom control may duplicate something the design system already solved. The cost moves downstream into QA, accessibility testing or production fixes.
  2. Prompt harder. Tell the model to use semantic HTML, support keyboard navigation and use the design system. Better than nothing, but every developer and agent has to remember the wording, and prompt templates silently go stale as the design system evolves. In her words, a prompt is still a request, not an enforcement mechanism.
  3. Change the environment. Make approved components, test utilities, Storybook examples and CI checks part of the architecture. Instead of asking for an accessible modal, give the model a modal component that already handles focus and keyboard behaviour.

Her rule of thumb for what to encode: if a requirement is stable, repeatable and important enough that you'd reject a pull request over it, look for the part of it that can be automated.

Defence in depth for the frontend

She describes the guardrails as a stack where no single layer has to be perfect. Composition steers code toward approved components; she calls a mature design system a policy engine expressed as reusable code, with APIs that make the common case easy. Storybook makes forgotten states (errors, loading, empty, focus, responsive layouts) part of the component contract, and doubles as better context for an AI assistant than bare TypeScript types. Playwright checks real flows: tab through the form, open the dialog, close it with Escape, get focus back where it belongs. axe-core catches structural, rule-based issues. CI turns all of it into a delivery rule.

Two craft notes stand out. Test user outcomes (the error is announced, focus moves correctly) rather than DOM structure, so the implementation can change. And make failures actionable: a gate that just says the accessibility check failed is bureaucracy, while one that names the rule and the element is help.

Honest about the limits

Niharika is careful with claims. Architectural guardrails cost upfront platform investment and maintenance; they pay off for standards that recur across teams, less so for a one-off experiment. An automated scan is one layer of evidence, not proof of accessibility: tools can tell you a control has no name, not whether the name is right or whether a screen reader user can finish the task. Manual and assistive-technology testing still matter.

Her starting point needs no new programme: look at recurring PR comments, accessibility bugs and patterns teams keep reinventing, and move one stable expectation into a component, a Playwright helper or a CI check. Over time the platform becomes a memory system for engineering lessons, which matters more when agents multiply whatever patterns they find.

Who should watch

Frontend leads and design-system owners whose teams already use coding assistants, and accessibility advocates looking for an argument platform teams will buy. It's conceptual rather than a live build, with the tooling named and the trade-offs spelled out.

entry.title: Personalised RAG should change the answer's shape, never its numbers
entry.summary: Santosh Muthyala (Meta) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026 on RAG for analytics that adapts to engineers, analysts and PMs while facts stay fixed.
entry.content:
A data engineer, a business analyst and a product manager ask the same question: why did checkout conversion drop last week? At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026, Santosh Muthyala, Data Engineering Manager at Meta, argued that a RAG system should give them three different answers built on one set of facts. Personalise the evidence emphasis and the presentation; never the metric definition, the numbers, the uncertainty or the access rights.

Grounded isn't the same as useful

RAG grounds an analytics answer in metric definitions, schemas, documentation and queries. That settles whether the answer is supported. It doesn't settle whether it helps the reader: several paragraphs of SQL detail don't help a PM, and a tidy business summary leaves an engineer unable to reproduce the result. Personalisation is aimed at that second question while keeping the first intact.

His hypothetical e-commerce example runs through the whole talk. Conversion is completed checkouts over eligible checkout starts, comparing two full weeks. Overall it falls from 5% to 4.5%; mobile drops from 6% to 5% while desktop holds at 4%, with 10,000 checkout starts per device each week.

Three work products from one set of evidence

The engineer gets the query, the metric definition, session-level counts, lineage and assumptions, plus a flag when validation checks haven't actually run. The system doesn't pretend they passed.

The analyst gets the headline drop, the device breakdown pointing at mobile, and a lead: the mobile payment error rate rose from 2% to 3.5%, marked as not yet validated. A hypothesis to investigate, not a root cause.

The product manager gets the impact framed as a 10% relative drop and 100 fewer completed sessions, suggested next steps, likely owners in checkout and payments, and links to the dashboards. Nobody gets a different number because a simpler summary would read better, and nobody gets a cause presented as confirmed when it isn't.

Profiles hold hints, not rules

The architecture has three components with explicit contracts: a user profile store that supplies hints, a retrieval system that supplies permitted evidence with enough context to interpret it, and a personalised generation layer that produces the answer in the right format.

Santosh's profile rules are the most transferable part. Keep it minimal: preferred tools, familiar domains, role, preferred depth. Record where each attribute came from: declared by the user, supplied by an application, or inferred. The current request wins over history, so a summary-lover who asks for SQL gets SQL. Users can inspect, correct and reset their preferences. And familiarity with a dataset never grants access to it; authorisation stays a separate decision.

Eligible first, then useful

Retrieval draws on five logical indices that can live in one store: schemas, documentation, metric definitions, past queries and curated SQL examples. Before ranking, an eligibility stage drops sources that are similar but inappropriate (another business unit, another environment, outside the user's permissions) and weighs authority: a canonical definition and an informal investigation note aren't equals. When sources conflict, the system should surface the conflict instead of quietly picking one.

Ranking then orders the eligible evidence by relevance, task fit and freshness. His line on it is a good one to tape to a monitor: usefulness doesn't override authority. A popular query blaming payment errors can't replace the canonical conversion definition.

Roll it out in phases, and prove it helps

His rollout order is foundation first (sources, metadata, access controls), then a RAG system that serves the current task before inferring anything about the user, then editable preferences. Evaluation covers retrieval, answers, drift (an old profile shouldn't keep steering someone whose job changed) and safety (prompt injection, query-history exposure, cross-tenant leakage). Keep a non-personalised baseline so you can tell whether personalisation is helping at all, and keep humans in the loop for consequential actions: suggesting an investigation differs from executing a rollback.

Who should watch

Data platform teams building natural-language analytics, and anyone whose RAG assistant serves very different roles from one index. The example data is hypothetical, so treat it as a design pattern with clear contracts rather than a production results talk.

entry.title: PayPal moves the compliance gate onto the paved road with MCP
entry.summary: Sumeet L. Ram (PayPal) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on exposing a geo-expansion platform to agents over MCP while people keep approving the rules.
entry.content:
On most paved roads the compliance check sits at the very end, where it's most expensive to fail. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, Sumeet L. Ram, Senior Technical Product Manager at PayPal who owns the geo-expansion platform teams use to launch in new markets, showed how to move that gate into the road itself by exposing the platform to AI agents through a Model Context Protocol server, with people still approving every rule.

His closing line is the whole talk in six words: agents find and flag, people decide.

The platform had the answer; nobody asked

Sumeet opens with a story most platform owners will recognise. A team integrates through the platform SDK; it works. Compliance adds a new data-handling rule for some markets; the platform ships support, with release notes. The team's integration still works, so nobody looks. Weeks later an audit asks, and the scramble begins.

More than 150 product teams use his platform to launch in a new market by configuration rather than rebuilding. Yet teams build for their home market first, discover market rules late in the sprint, file a ticket and wait, each reading the docs their own way. The same five failures repeat: teams stuck on old versions, one requirement built five ways, compliance gaps found after code is written, a single missed rule holding up a launch, and real exposure in regulated flows. Regulators and payment networks change rules on their own calendars, which never match sprint plans. End-of-life notices meet the eternal promise to upgrade next quarter.

Now add agents. A team's agent working off a PRD and Figma files will figure out market rules on its own, confidently, sometimes even correctly, and ungoverned.

Three tools any platform can offer an agent

The fix is an MCP server in front of the platform, so rules show up at design time instead of at release. Sumeet's core slide, and the one he asks you to remember, is three kinds of tools:

  1. Adopt: how do I build on this, or move to the current version?
  2. Update: what changed that affects my flow?
  3. Verify: is my work still valid, checked before launch and long after?

His example is address layout. Some markets write addresses from the largest administrative unit down; the West goes street first. With the platform reachable by agents, the integration gets it right from day one and nothing surprises QA during KYC or KYB checks. He notes the pattern fits any rule-heavy platform: security, accessibility, data handling.

When agents become your customers

Once the platform speaks MCP, other agents start asking it first. A design tool's agent can ask which layouts change by market, so designs match what production will really render, and QA stops comparing a home-market mock to a localised screen. A policy agent can watch the compliance system of record, compare it to what's live, notify the owning team and open a pull request with the fix, which a person reviews before anything ships.

Governance runs in two loops that meet in the platform's rule set. Teams read it at design time. Custodians maintain it: a recurring research loop scans standards bodies and regulators, scores how well current rules still match, and proposes updates when the score drops, and a platform custodian approves every change. That approval is what makes the audit trail credible: each answer carries the rule version, its source, its effective date and who approved it, so you can answer an auditor asking why the platform said what it said on a given day.

Numbers, with honest caveats

Sumeet says he has seen up to a 96% reduction in upgrade time, and gives a directional range of roughly 50 to 80% less effort across finding rules, upgrading and keeping rules current, while telling you to measure your own. His five moves to copy: find your late loop, expose the platform where work starts, offer adopt/update/verify tools, make upgrades the platform's job, and keep people owning the rules. Start with the rule that changed most recently.

Who should watch

Owners of any platform with rules attached (payments, privacy, security, accessibility) who are watching agents start to consume their APIs. It's a product-manager talk about operating model rather than MCP server code.

entry.title: MazeWall lets a JVM app sandbox its own threads with seccomp
entry.summary: Leanid Piliptsevich (EPAM) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 introduces MazeWall, using seccomp and Landlock to restrict pieces of an app from inside.
entry.content:
Your image-resizing function has the same right to read secrets as the rest of your process. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, Leanid Piliptsevich, Java developer at EPAM, introduced MazeWall, an experimental open-source research project that lets JVM applications restrict individual threads and processes with Linux kernel tools, so a bug in one small piece of logic can't take the whole app with it.

It's a short talk, and an introduction rather than a production case study. Leanid is clear about that, and about the limits.

Containers see one big app

Leanid's starting point: applications talk to Linux constantly, and Linux has strong security subsystems, but it can only act on the information the app gives it. Containers use those same subsystems and you should keep using them. Yet a container sees your service as one monolith and applies one policy to all of it.

Developers don't see their apps that way. We think in modules, classes and methods. He compares the goal to a warship's compartments: a breach in one shouldn't sink the vessel. Today, to the kernel and to an attacker, one flaw is enough to compromise everything. Take that image resizer: there's no code in it that reads secrets, until a crafted input exploits a bug and adds some.

Profile first, then lock the thread

MazeWall's workflow has two halves. First, profile the logic you'll run in production and record every Linux system call it makes, in the new Software Bill of Behavior format, which Leanid clearly enjoys. Second, turn that bill of behaviour into a policy and apply it to the thread or process that runs the logic. Anything the profile saw keeps working; anything it didn't, fails.

Enforcement then belongs to the kernel, through seccomp for syscalls and Landlock for filesystem access. MazeWall's job ends once the policy is applied, which removes the confused-deputy problem of a userspace guard. One property shapes how you design with it: once a policy is applied you can't relax or remove it. Need different permissions? Start a new thread or process with a new policy. Per the abstract, the JDK Foreign Function and Memory API is how a Java or Kotlin app reaches those kernel interfaces.

Threads are convenient, processes are safer

Leanid lays out three scopes. Process isolation is the proven one; he points out that the Elastic team has used it internally for about ten years and credits that approach with limiting Log4j-style attacks. Thread scope is the developer-friendly option and lets you restrict really small units of logic, since an app has one process but many threads. Its fundamental weakness is shared memory, so some attacks get through. The third option, spawning a dedicated worker process for the risky logic, trades convenience for that stronger isolation. His recommendation is to combine thread and process restrictions rather than pick one.

Who should watch

JVM engineers who parse untrusted input (documents, images, archives) and security-minded platform teams who already squeezed what they can out of container policies. It's a brief, basic tour; the details live in the MazeWall repository, linked from the talk. Don't expect benchmarks or a deployment story yet.

entry.title: Prompt contracts catch the one-word edit that flips the meaning
entry.summary: Sachin Gupta (eBay) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026 on prompt contracts, the schema, claim, tool and policy checks that stop prompt drift in CI.
entry.content:
"Debug logs are retained for 14 days" and "debug logs are not retained for 14 days" differ by one word, and in Sachin Gupta's demo the second one sailed through every check until he added the right one. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026, Sachin, Member of Technical Staff at eBay, presented prompt contracts: turning the clauses of a prompt into written requirements, each backed by an automated check, so drift shows up in CI instead of in user complaints.

Stable doesn't mean identical

His definition of drift is behavioural: a prompt-driven app moving away from its intended behaviour when the instructions or the surrounding conditions change. The running example is an IT assistant explaining debug log retention from a policy that says 14 days. "Debug logs are retained for fourteen days" and "we keep the debug logs for fourteen days" are both fine. Seven days, or "not retained", is not.

So stability means the requirements still hold under the changes you're testing, not that the wording never moves. And if the approved policy changes, the expected answer changes with it; the test follows the requirement, never the other way round.

The harmless tone edit

The revision under examination is the kind every team makes: add a warmer, more reassuring tone for the engineer filing the incident. Reasonable intent, real risk. Reassurance can mean acknowledging the concern and saying the incident will be investigated; it must not become a promise that it will be resolved.

His clearer prompt names the boundaries explicitly: the task and evidence (explain retention from the supplied policy, preserve the period), the style boundary (supportive, without promising an outcome), the fallback (return insufficient evidence rather than guessing), and named output fields including a citation with an exact source quotation. He's careful to say rewritten wording is a design decision, not proof it works; its effect still needs evidence.

Each clause becomes a check

The contract maps prompt to test. Required JSON becomes a schema check on fields and types. Exact source quotes become a check that the source exists and contains the quotation. No resolution guarantee becomes a forbidden-phrase check, which he admits has limited coverage. Preserving the policy meaning needs a separate check on the claim itself. Passing one row proves nothing about the others.

For comparisons, decide before editing which examples should pass and fail (normal requests, missing evidence, harmless paraphrases, boundary-pushing instructions), keep fresh cases outside the development set, run the unchanged baseline repeatedly first, and hold the model and generation settings fixed.

The six-tab demo

The demo app, with Java checks, walks through six tabs. The baseline passes. The tone edit produces "your incident is guaranteed to be resolved" and the forbidden-claim check blocks it. The tool boundary tab is the sneaky one: the answer and its shape are fine, but the agent tries to close a ticket when it only had permission to create one, so the tool contract gate fails. Drift, he points out, isn't only in the text; tool calling drifts too.

Then the meaning escape: "not retained" gets released, because no bounded policy check existed. Add one and it's withheld. The final trade-off tab is a creative paraphrase that keeps the meaning; the system withholds it for human review rather than auto-passing something it can't confidently recognise.

A CI fixture suite ties it together: a valid control passes; forbidden guarantees, wrong tool, wrong tool version, wrong call order and policy contradictions fail; valid paraphrases and missing-evidence cases (where no tool should be called) pass.

Who should watch

Teams shipping LLM features that talk about policy, support or anything with facts a user will act on, and anyone who has tweaked a prompt for tone and wondered what else changed. The demo uses prepared examples, so it shows the checks working rather than a measured comparison across live generations; Sachin says as much.

entry.title: T-Mobile treats the T-Life app shell as an internal platform
entry.summary: RanjithKumar Ragavan (T-Mobile) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on how five teams ship into one 53-million-user mobile app without breaking each other.
entry.content:
In the backend, giving five teams independence means five repos and five deploys. In a mobile app, Apple and Google take exactly one binary, so everyone compiles, links and ships together. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, RanjithKumar Ragavan, Member of Technical Staff leading mobile architecture for T-Mobile's T-Life app, showed how his team turned that single binary into a self-service internal platform for five engineering pods and 50-plus mobile engineers.

The numbers set the stakes: T-Life serves 53 million active users, millions open it at once on T-Mobile Tuesdays to claim rewards, and the team holds itself to a crash-free session rate above 99.9%.

One super app, five teams, one junk drawer

T-Life replaced a set of separate apps (bill pay, rewards, home internet) with one. Customers liked it. Engineering inherited one binary, five teams and nothing between them. The loyalty team imported account internals to check login; IoT reached straight into payment code; shared folders became a place where everyone dumped helper classes. A change to one shared file in payments broke compilation for loyalty, and one broken test could block every engineer at the same time.

The organisational fix came first. Four feature pods (account, payments, loyalty, IoT) serve customers. The fifth, the core shell pod, owns navigation, dependency injection, analytics and other infrastructure, and its customers are the other four teams. The shell holds no business logic; its job is to be a stable foundation that features plug into.

Contracts small enough to compile in a second

The central mechanism is versioned interface contracts. Every team splits its module into a tiny contract module (interfaces and data models only, no UI, no database) and a private implementation. The rule: depend on other teams' contract modules, never on their implementations. Contracts use semantic versioning. A non-breaking addition is a minor bump nobody notices; a breaking change means deprecating the old method, shipping a new contract version and giving consumers time to move. Behind the contract, a team can rewrite internals or redesign screens without telling anyone.

That separation makes isolated builds possible. When a payments PR lands, CI compiles only payments against the prebuilt contracts, runs its unit and UI tests and quality checks, then passes a gate that also verifies the public contract wasn't accidentally broken. Only then is the new version promoted into app integration. If payments fails the gate, the others keep shipping on the last good payments version. Ranjith reports zero cross-team build regressions across all five pods, and feedback in a couple of minutes instead of waiting on a monolith build.

Plug, don't wire

Features join the app through modular feature injection, which he compares to a wall socket: the electrician doesn't need to know whether you'll plug in a kettle or a TV. Each feature module ships a registration file declaring its screens, deep links and the platform services it needs. At startup the shell scans the registry and connects features at runtime. When a user taps "pay bill" on home, the home screen asks the shell to open a route; it knows nothing about payment code. Teams register, wrap the feature in a remote flag and release on their own schedule, without waiting for the shell team.

Governance by linter, state by event bus

Two risks remain when teams move fast: someone bypasses the rules under a deadline, or modules corrupt each other at runtime. For the first, no review board. Changes inside your own module need zero outside approvals; changing a shared public contract needs a short RFC; an automated lint rule fails the pull request if loyalty imports payment's private code; and an ADR log in the repo records why each rule exists.

For runtime, each module uses MVI or MVVM with one-directional state flow. Modules never call each other directly: on logout, account publishes an event to a shared bus and every module clears its own data. State is scoped to a module's lifecycle, so closing the IoT screens frees IoT's memory. Ranjith ties that hygiene directly to keeping the crash-free rate.

Who should watch

Mobile architects on any app with more than two teams in one codebase, and backend platform engineers who want to see contracts, isolated pipelines and self-service land in a world with a single deployable. It's architecture and process rather than code, delivered with plenty of slide metaphors.

entry.title: A plan span catches the agent that got the right answer by luck
entry.summary: Krishna Chaitanya Balusu (Meta) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026 on OpenTelemetry plan spans for debugging agent prompts, not just answers.
entry.content:
The run that worries Krishna Chaitanya Balusu most is the one where the agent's answer is right and its plan is wrong. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026, Krishna, a Senior Software Engineer at Meta who builds AI agents for incident response, showed how to record an agent's plan as an OpenTelemetry span and check it next to the answer, so a lucky shortcut fails the build before it fails a user.

He has standing to say it: he contributed the plan operation to the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions, and he built AgentTelemetry, a benchmark for finding faults in agent traces published at ACM AIware.

Agents break the prompt feedback loop

With a single-turn prompt you change the wording, read the output and judge it, ten rounds in a few minutes. An agent plans, calls tools and then answers, and you still only see the answer. You can't see which tools it chose or which step it skipped, so you tweak the prompt and hope. In the title's words, you cannot fix a prompt you cannot see fail.

The release helper with two plans

His running example is small enough to hold in your head. A release helper answers "is this release ready to ship?" with three tools: read summary (yesterday's summary, fast but stale), read manifest (today's required checks) and read checks (today's results). Ready if every required check passes, blocked if one fails, unknown if the evidence is missing.

Plan A reads the summary and says ready. Plan B reads the manifest, then the checks, and says ready. Today both pass the answer check. Tomorrow a security check fails: plan B says blocked, plan A still says ready, because it never looked.

Record the plan, then test it

A plan span records the operation name (plan), the agent's name and the plan itself; in the demo the plan is a list of the tools the agent decided to call. Each tool call then gets its own execute-tool span. He keeps the payload tiny (no full prompts, no long reasoning) and is clear about what it is: the plan your app got back from the model, not a window into the model's mind. The conventions are still marked development, so pin the version.

Once the plan is recorded, checking it is a normal test: does the plan include the manifest and the checks, in that order? Pass or fail. No plan span at all is unknown, never pass.

Why a shared name matters: every framework logs planning its own way, if at all. In his benchmark, standard OpenTelemetry plus the GenAI conventions caught 6 of 14 fault types, and planning failure was among the missed ones because there was nothing to look at. With agent-specific spans including planning, the reference setup caught all 14. He flags that it's a controlled benchmark.

The demo, in Jaeger

The demo runs the helper five times with scripted plans, real OpenTelemetry spans sent to Jaeger, and no model calls, so it runs on a laptop without an API key. One table, four checks per run: answer, plan, tools, and whether today's evidence was read. The answer-passes row shows the trap: the answer is correct, but the plan span lists only the summary tool.

The other rows separate failures that look the same from outside. A tool timeout has a good plan, an error on the tool span and the honest answer unknown, so you fix the tool, not the prompt. A missing plan span means fixing instrumentation before drawing conclusions. The stale-summary day is when the shortcut finally bites, and the plan check had already flagged that workflow on the good day.

Turning the trace into a better prompt

The fix maps straight to the trace. Version one only asked the agent to check release readiness and return ready or blocked. It named no source of evidence, so reading the old summary was a fair way to obey it. Version two names the current release manifest, asks for every required check, and says what to return when evidence is missing. Then treat it as an experiment: same model, tools and cases; many runs, since models are random; score plan and answer separately; and keep every failure as a permanent test case.

Who should watch

Anyone iterating on prompts for agents with a real planning or routing step, and observability folks wondering what GenAI semantic conventions buy them. It's tightly scoped and demo-driven: the plan is scripted, so how often a real model plans correctly is the measurement he leaves to you.

entry.title: With AI coding, the delivery bottleneck moves to code review
entry.summary: Lucas Mazei (Memed) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 applies the theory of constraints to AI-assisted delivery and shows where platform teams should push.
entry.content:
If your coding stage just doubled its output and your throughput didn't move, Eliyahu Goldratt would like a word. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, Lucas Mateus Mazei Sobrinho, engineering manager at the Brazilian health tech Memed, walked through the theory of constraints applied to AI-assisted software delivery, and why the fastest way to look productive (approve more PRs) is also the fastest way to drown in rework.

Five boxes and a queue

Lucas starts with a deliberately simple model: five stages (implementation, review, validation, release, production) with illustrative fixed capacities of 4, 3, 4, 4 and 4 changes a day. Review handles three, so the whole system finishes three a day. Speed up release to six or seven and nothing changes, because release only ever receives three. Local optimisation of a non-bottleneck is theatre.

Then he applies AI. Implementation capacity goes up, but so does the size of each pull request: one PR can now hold a whole feature, several times a day. In his model review drops from three to two, and work piles up waiting in the PR list. He says he's hearing exactly this from other managers, tech leads and staff engineers.

The wrong fix: rubber-stamp it

The tempting move is to review faster by reviewing less. Suppose tired reviewers start approving ten a day. The review queue clears in a flash, and validation becomes the pile. Worse, the poorly reviewed changes start coming back: feature 17 fails validation and returns as a rework ticket; feature 18 breaks in production and does the same. Each repair goes through implementation, review and validation again, consuming the same finite attention as new work.

His accounting rule is worth pinning up: a repair is another attempt at an existing outcome, so link it to the original and never count the outcome twice. Six approvals are not six outcomes.

The right fix: make review smaller, not sloppier

This is where Lucas gets platform-specific. Before a human or a model looks at a change, run deterministic quality gates against the base revision: same lint rules and test configuration, checks for introduced duplication, coverage drops and broken end-to-end flows. A failed gate feeds a repair agent straight away. Once the gates pass, an AI reviewer looks at behaviour, context and risk, and its findings feed the same repair agent. Every repair is a new revision that restarts the gates.

Two constraints keep it honest. The agent can't lower a threshold or weaken an assertion to get to green. And the loop is bounded (his example: two repair attempts or ten minutes) before it hands the finding and evidence to a person. Tools like CodeRabbit and Linear then help reviewers focus on the parts that need judgment.

He also argues for generators over generated code. If a NestJS resource generator or your own CLI produces the model, controller, service, DTO and test skeleton, and you approved the schema and use case, nobody needs to read the boilerplate. That saves review time and, as a bonus, tokens.

Then do it again

Fix review and validation becomes the constraint, so Lucas suggests agents that use the product like a user, with repeatable Playwright tests, or engineers owning validation outright. Then release, then production. The constraint isn't always the next column on the board; it can be a shared specialist or a decision nobody is making.

Measurement follows the whole path: completed outcomes with comparable scope, elapsed time, age of unfinished work, escaped defects, change failures, rework and recovery. And count AI cost per useful outcome rather than per line written. The reading list is two books: Goldratt's The Goal and Dominica DeGrandis's Making Work Visible.

Who should watch

Engineering managers whose dashboards show more PRs and the same releases, and platform teams deciding where to invest in an AI-assisted pipeline. If you already live by value-stream maps, the first act is review; the gates-plus-bounded-repair-loop design is the new part.

entry.title: A detailed prompt still doesn't make the answer correct
entry.summary: Emmanuela Opurum (SoftNet Technologies) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026 on templates, .md rule files and evaluating every AI response.
entry.content:
Claude builds your first page beautifully, so you trust it with the second, and the second quietly pulls in a package your project never uses. That scenario sits at the centre of Emmanuela Opurum's talk at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026. Emmanuela, a Solutions Architect at SoftNet Technologies, argues that prompt engineering is the evaluation around the prompt as much as the prompt itself: a good result yesterday earns no trust for today's output.

It's a practical, beginner-friendly talk aimed at people using Claude, Codex and similar tools day to day, not a framework or tooling showcase.

Prompting vs prompt engineering

Her definitions are simple. Prompting is the instruction you give an agent to get a response. Prompt engineering adds the workflow around it: knowing the project's requirements and standards, and checking every result against them. The trap she names is believing that more detail in the prompt makes the output automatically correct. It doesn't; it only makes it more likely to be shaped the way you want.

Her corollary is blunt: if you don't know what success looks like for the project before you start, you have no business handing the work to an AI, because you'd have nothing to evaluate against.

Keep the stable parts in a file

The most reusable habit is how she structures prompts. The things that never change in a project (the role, coding style, rules, policies) go into a template, or into the .md instruction files that Claude and Codex read. The chat box then carries only the task at hand. You stop repeating yourself, and the agent stops guessing your standards.

She's careful to add that a reusable template saves prompting time but doesn't produce identical results. Every output still gets checked.

Relevant context beats more context

Detailed doesn't mean dumping everything. Her example is the CV request: paste a job description and ask the model to build your CV around it, without giving it your experience or skills, and it will invent a candidate for you. The fix is the missing context plus an example, such as an existing CV in the format you like. Irrelevant context, on the other hand, confuses the agent. The model will happily fill any gap you leave, which is the problem.

Test the cases you didn't think about

Evaluation, for her, is more than the happy path. Test missing fields, partial changes, conflicting instructions and edge cases, and keep running the same test cases every time you update a prompt. She credits that discipline with stopping a prompt that looked fine in several tries from reaching her production build. It's also what lets you answer a lead who asks why you shipped that code.

Drift: change one line at a time

Her approach to prompt drift is small-step debugging. When the generated page is great except the footer you asked for is missing, she edits only the line that describes the footer, re-runs, and re-evaluates, rather than rewriting the whole prompt. Once it works, the prompt gets saved as a template for similar tasks.

Secrets never go in the chat box

She closes on security: no API keys, client data, or personal or bank details pasted into a prompt. Keys belong in the platform's secret store; she uses GitHub's secrets for the integrations in her projects.

Who should watch

Developers and analysts who've moved from occasional chats to relying on an agent for real project work and want a sane routine, and team leads looking for plain-language guidance to hand to newer colleagues. If you already run eval suites and versioned prompts in CI, this will be familiar ground; the related talks below go further into the tooling.

entry.title: A platform team of one runs side projects with AI, not on AI
entry.summary: Shem Magnezi (Lemonade) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on running many AI-built side projects alone with minimal launches, recoverable paths and agents.
entry.content:
Coding agents made building cheap. They did not make running a product cheap. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, Shem Magnezi, Senior Staff Engineer at Lemonade and former CTO of the startup Wilco, framed his habit of shipping a side project almost every month as a platform-engineering problem with a team size of one: cut repeated work, make delegation usable, and decide what actually deserves a human.

It's a personal, practical talk, and the most useful parts are his failures.

The agent will give you the average idea

Shem tested the beach-and-beer fantasy directly. He asked an agent to brainstorm fifty product ideas, pick the best one and run with it, with a small budget and no involvement from him. After more than 24 hours it came back with very basic ideas that got no traction and no income. His conclusion: AI is good at proposing and building, but its ideas, designs and go-to-market plans gravitate to the average. Judgment and context stay with you.

So he pivoted to building things he needed himself, which also supplies the motivation to finish. One example: a Chrome extension to find FIFA World Cup tickets. Scraping FIFA's site turned into a cat-and-mouse game that FIFA won every time, and the agent was (rightly) conservative about workarounds. Shem's own fix was to make it a portal where almost a thousand users each looked up their own data, and the aggregate gave everyone a picture of availability. No agent proposed that.

Ship the minimum, but protect the recoverable path

His second lesson is about where to spend scarce attention. He used to polish every feature (load, non-English users, power users) for projects that then got no users. Now the first version should take an hour if possible. For a service that turns an old photo into an emotional video, version one was a landing page asking for an email and an image, with Shem doing the work by hand.

Only after a few dozen real orders did he build automation and run ads. Then one TikTok campaign took off overnight, the site fell over under the load, and he lost orders. He still thinks the trade was worth it, but he wished he had load-tested with an agent first and kept the emails so he could follow up.

He learned. On a later Disney World queue-time assistant, the very first paying user hit a broken billing flow, paid and got nothing. Because the email was captured, Shem could fix it and make it right. The rule: things will break, so make sure the paths that matter are recoverable. And every project gets a back office he can drive from his phone: contact users, edit what they received, see and fix errors from a bus.

Act like a CEO, let the reports find you

The third lesson is the operating model. Shem built a board, somewhere between Trello and Slack, where his agents work. He sets goals at the level of five features by the end of the week, agents break them down, and he approves direction rather than reviewing PRs or Helm chart diffs. Recurring work (say, five new articles every Monday) runs on a schedule as a cron or weekly worker in Claude Code instead of waiting for a reminder.

Guardrails are non-negotiable: caps on cost and tokens, because nobody wants a surprise four-figure bill from a hobby. Agents propose, he gives a thumbs up or down. And information flows the other way from usual: he doesn't open logs, alerts or Datadog; daily and weekly reports push to him, mostly quiet, ideally empty.

Who should watch

Engineers with a day job and a folder of half-finished ideas, and platform people curious how golden-path thinking scales down to one person and a fleet of agents. Shem is candid that he hasn't quit his job or got rich; the payoff he describes is skills, tools he brought back to work, and World Cup tickets. If you want hard benchmarks on agent frameworks, look elsewhere.

entry.title: The smallest internal platform: a plugin-based Dev Mode for Android
entry.summary: Denis Galkin (Robofinance) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on turning scattered debug menus into a plugin-based Dev Mode framework inside the app.
entry.content:
Every mobile app grows a hidden button on the profile screen, a debug menu in settings and a secret gesture somewhere else. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, Denis Galkin, Android engineer at Robofinance, showed how his team treated those internal tools as a platform product from the start: a plugin-based Dev Mode framework where the framework owns the shell and the app owns every tool inside it.

It's a platform talk at the scale of one binary, and the lessons travel well beyond Android.

Split the shell from the content

The classic platform problem, Denis argues, happens inside one app too: people build the same thing many times, differently, and nobody owns the result. Developers redo navigation for each new tool, QA has to remember where every tool lives (or interrupt a developer), and each app ends up with its own debug menu.

Dev Mode's core idea is a hard split. The framework owns activation, the Dev Mode screen, the list of tools and navigation between them. The app owns which tools exist, their screens, view models, repositories and settings. The framework has no idea what mock date or test push means; to it, every tool is a name and a screen. Denis compares it to Backstage: a small core with everything useful in plugins.

Why bother? Because the two halves change at different speeds. The shell almost never changes once it works; the content changes every sprint. Keep them apart and the shared code stays quiet.

No when statement in the framework

The walkthrough is concrete. Activation is one line in the app: initDevModeListener on a View, or a Modifier.devModeClickable in Jetpack Compose. A Dev Mode Runner inside the framework counts taps (five by default, with a timer that resets the count) and opens Dev Mode Activity.

That activity depends on one interface, IDevModePluginEntriesProvider, whose single method returns entries for Navigation 3, Google's new navigation library. The app implements it, registering screens like TestPushesDevPluginScreen and MockDatePluginScreen. A second small interface supplies the menu: an index, a title and a screen key per plugin. The router takes a key and navigates. Denis's favourite detail: there's no Kotlin when anywhere in the framework deciding which tool to open. The framework builds the route; the app decides where it leads.

Adding a tool (say, a feature flag switcher) is four steps, all inside the app: screen plus view model, navigation key, registration, menu item. The framework isn't touched. In his phrasing, the cost of a new tool should be the cost of the tool, not the platform around it.

Adopted without a migration

The adoption story is the part platform teams should study. Nobody was told to use Dev Mode, and there was no migration. Denis gives three reasons. Timing: the framework arrived before ad-hoc tools spread, so there was nothing to move and no owners to persuade. The easy way was the right way: registering a plugin beats building your own debug screen. And ownership follows the feature: whoever builds a feature builds its test plugin in the same task.

Users turned out to be broader than dev suggests. QA sets up dates and pushes without a special build; managers check app behaviour on their own. With weekly releases, that's everyday work, not an edge case.

What he'd do differently

Two honest regrets. Measure from day one (time to prepare a test scenario, how often QA needs a developer), because preventing a problem leaves you no before chart to show anyone. And name an owner for the core before plugin screens drift apart and dead tools pile up in the list. For small or short-lived apps he'd skip the full framework but keep one rule: a single entry point for all internal tools.

Who should watch

Mobile leads with more than one debug menu, and platform engineers who want a clean, small example of a golden path that people choose without being told. If you think platform engineering only means Kubernetes, this is a good corrective.

entry.title: A looping agent keeps every dashboard green
entry.summary: Indika Wimalasuriya (Virtusa) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026 traces a Bedrock AgentCore agent end to end in Datadog, kill switch included.
entry.content:
It's 3am, p95 latency is fine, the error rate is 0.2% and CPU sits at 34%, while the agent underneath calls the same tool over and over with hallucinated arguments. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026, Indika Wimalasuriya, Director of SRE and Observability at Virtusa, showed how to see that kind of failure by wiring an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent into Datadog, and how to stop it with a kill switch built before go-live.

The talk is a vendor-specific build (AWS plus Datadog) with a working demo and the configuration traps he hit along the way, which is the most reusable part.

Healthy infrastructure, unhealthy agent

Indika's starting point: the old question "is it running?" barely matters for an agent that reasons, picks tools, reads results and acts, and might take two steps today and seven tomorrow. Loops, wrong arguments, conversations drifting away from what the user asked, token burn and actions that succeed while doing the wrong thing raise no traditional alert at all.

So on top of metrics, logs and traces he wants six more signals: the decision trace, tool invocation spans, token cost per step, model behaviour (stop reasons, errors, throttles), session and memory state, and guardrail evaluations.

The reference architecture

The demo is an insurance assistant built with the Strands Agents SDK on AgentCore Runtime, using a Claude model on Bedrock and six in-process Python tools: policy lookup, claim status, filing a claim, policyholder lookup, weather risk and a repair cost estimator. The browser carries Datadog Real User Monitoring and calls API Gateway plus a small Lambda proxy that holds the IAM permission to invoke the agent. The agent sends OpenTelemetry traces and logs straight to Datadog's intake with no collector in the path; the Lambda uses the Datadog extension, and the web host runs a normal Datadog agent.

Three steps and the hours they cost

Keep AgentCore's built-in instrumentation (the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry) on, register a Datadog OTLP exporter in code next to it, and opt spans into LLM Observability while emitting the GenAI semantic conventions (version 1.37 or later). The heads-up box is where he lost a few hours: setting the standard OTLP exporter environment variables got 403s from Datadog, and only registering the exporter in code worked. Without the LLM Observability flag everything appears in APM and the AI view stays empty. And the app name comes from the root span's service name, not the variable you'd expect.

Read the trace before optimising

A real trace for "how much would it cost to repair a dented bumper?" ran about six seconds. Nearly all of it was the model thinking; the repair estimator failed once with service unavailable in about 30 milliseconds, the second LLM call decided to retry, and the retry succeeded. Two lessons fall out: if you want the agent faster, the tools are not where to look, and without the trace you'd see one slow request that worked.

APM answers where the time went, LLM Observability what the agent decided, infrastructure whether the platform is healthy, and logs what exactly failed. Shared trace IDs plus consistent service, environment and version tags let you pivot between them.

Build the kill switch first

Failed calls are loud; unexpected calls (wrong tool, out-of-range parameters, the same tool again and again) are quiet. A runaway loop raised zero errors in the demo; only the tool-call rate and token count gave it away. So: track tokens per session by agent, model and tool, tag by team and environment, and alert on rate of change rather than a fixed number.

The demo's kill switch is concrete. An alarm on more than four tool calls a minute invokes a Lambda that flips an SSM parameter; every tool checks it and returns "suspended" for 90 seconds. He's honest about the limits: it's global, pausing every user, and because the alarm evaluates once a minute it stops the next turn, not the one that tripped it. A switch that pauses everyone beats an invoice that surprises everyone.

He closes with example SLOs for agents: task success, p95 session latency, tool error rate, cost per session within twice the baseline, and guardrail trigger rates alerting in both directions.

Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers who've been handed an agent in production, and anyone on AgentCore or Datadog who wants the exporter gotchas before losing the same afternoon. Teams on other stacks still get the signal list, the soft-failure lesson and the kill switch pattern.

entry.title: Kafka won't make your retail supply chain resilient on its own
entry.summary: Nidhin Jose (Walmart) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on the ownership, idempotency and recovery patterns that make event-driven retail systems hold up.
entry.content:
Putting a message broker between your services doesn't remove failures; it moves them into asynchronous workflows where they're harder to see. That's the opening claim from Nidhin Jose, Staff Software Engineer at Walmart, at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, and the rest of his talk is a compact checklist of what actually makes an event-driven retail platform resilient, and which parts a platform team should own.

The setting is retail: one customer order crosses order management, inventory, fulfillment, logistics, stores and delivery. The customer sees one promise. Behind it sit many systems with different owners and different ways to break.

Publish only the facts you own

Resilience starts with ownership, not infrastructure. Order management owns the order lifecycle; inventory owns availability and reservations; logistics owns shipment progression. Each domain publishes only what it's authoritative for. Order management emits order placed; inventory answers with stock reserved or reservation rejected.

Nidhin draws a firm line between commands and events. Reserve stock is a command: intent, which can be refused. Stock reserved is an event: a recorded outcome. Blurring the two quietly rebuilds synchronous request-response over a message bus, with all the coupling and none of the honesty.

Assume every event arrives twice

On Kafka specifics, he keeps it precise. Producers don't wait for consumers; consumer groups move at their own pace. Partition by order ID and you get ordering within an order, not global ordering, a distinction that bites teams who assumed otherwise. Rebalances and retries mean reprocessing, so consumers must be safe against duplicates.

Two patterns carry the load:

  • Transactional outbox to close the dual-write gap: write the business update and the outgoing event in the same local transaction, and let a separate publisher deliver it. That fixes lost events but can still publish twice.
  • Idempotent consumers with stable event IDs and business-level checks, so processing stock reserved twice doesn't trigger two fulfillments.

Failures get classified too. Transient ones get bounded retries with back-off; invalid contracts or impossible states go to a dead-letter queue, and that queue needs an owner, alerting and controlled replay. A DLQ nobody reads is just a slower way to lose orders.

Use the heavy patterns selectively

Event sourcing, CQRS and sagas each get a fair, unhyped treatment. Event sourcing earns its keep where history matters, such as inventory receipts, reservations, releases and adjustments, but brings snapshots, schema evolution and retention costs. CQRS lets the storefront, the operator dashboard and analytics each get their own read model, at the price of lag, so critical decisions still check authoritative state. Sagas coordinate reserve, authorise payment and dispatch without a global transaction; compensation is a new business action (release the reservation, reroute, sometimes a human), not a database rollback.

Ordering is scoped, so a projection may see a logistics event before the related inventory update. Versions, transition rules, buffering or reconciliation handle that, and teams should know which views are authoritative and which may lag.

Where the platform team comes in

The platform owns the reusable mechanism; domains own the business logic. In Nidhin's paved path that means topic provisioning, schema registration, access control, producer and consumer templates, retries, DLQ handling, tracing, replay and contract testing. Event contracts get treated like APIs: adding an optional field is usually safe, removing or redefining one breaks consumers, and compatibility checks should catch that before production.

His adoption advice is refreshingly modest: start with one bounded business event, define owner, contract, consumers, failure modes and replay, then expand. And if a caller needs an immediate authoritative answer, a synchronous API may still be the right call.

Who should watch

Teams early in an event-driven migration, or platform engineers deciding what belongs in a shared eventing toolkit. It's a patterns talk without code or numbers, short and dense; seasoned Kafka operators will find it a good checklist rather than new territory.

entry.title: Five LLMs taught a small model to spot 70 kinds of news bias
entry.summary: Aleem Khan at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026 on replacing five LLM API calls per story with an owned model trained on expert-checked labels.
entry.content:
Aleem Khan's team started out thinking five frontier LLMs would be the product. They ended up as the teachers. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026, Aleem, an independent AI entrepreneur, told the story of a news pipeline that flags around 70 types of linguistic bias, and how it moved from asking OpenAI, Anthropic, Qwen, Grok and DeepSeek the same question about every story to a single in-house model that answers in one pass.

It's a talk about prompts as one component of a system: data collection, deduplication, domain experts, smaller specialist models and a retraining loop that never ends.

Bias you can't fact-check

The problem framing is sharp. Calling the same crowd protesters or rioters, choosing whose quote leads, leaving out context: none of it is fake news, and every fact can still be correct. You have to read the language itself. Trained linguists can do that for a few dozen articles a day; the news cycle produces thousands of stories an hour.

The pipeline pulls trending topics from X and then the full articles from Google News, because bias lives in headlines, lead paragraphs and quote order, not in tweets. Many outlets covering one event is the point: the contrast between "clashes" and "attack" is the signal.

Deduplication decides what the model learns

Stage two sounds boring and, Aleem says, shaped everything after it. Wire stories reposted word for word get grouped into one event, but the different outlets' versions are kept, since that comparison is the whole game. Follow-ups and analysis on day two and three are linked into one thread over time. Skip this and your dataset is dominated by the month's three biggest stories; the model learns what was in the news rather than how it was written.

When the prompt becomes an interface

The wrapper sent every story to five models with the same prompts and forced the same structured answer: which bias, where in the text, and why. Aleem's lesson for a prompt engineering crowd is that once more than one model is involved, the prompt is a contract that five very different systems have to honour, and the output format matters as much as the instructions.

The surprise was what the disagreements meant. When all five flag the same sentence, the bias is probably real. When two flag it and three don't, the text is either genuinely ambiguous or one model has a blind spot. Instead of averaging that away, the team treated it as a map of where human judgment was needed.

Linguists wrote the prompts

The humans were PhD linguists specialising in bias and hate speech, not crowd workers. They built the taxonomy (what separates loaded language from framing, or one-sided sourcing from omission), wrote the prompts with engineers turning them into something models follow reliably, chose which stories entered the dataset, and broke ties where the LLMs disagreed. A layer of small specialist models trained on public datasets acted as a second opinion, so every label passed through three filters before training.

After 11 months that produced roughly half a million stories, labelled for 70 biases and balanced across bias types, topics and outlets so rare biases had enough examples.

What the owned model does better

The trained model reads each sentence in the context of the whole article, checks all 70 biases in one pass on the team's own infrastructure, and returns spans, not a yes/no. Aleem's example is "The minister finally admitted the plan had failed." The model marks the loaded verb phrase, grades the severity, gives a short reason a human can accept or reject, and proposes a rewrite that says the minister reported the plan had not worked. It changes only the biased words, so the writer's voice survives, and the editor stays in charge.

Against the five-LLM pipeline it was more consistent (same input, same answer, which matters when you measure an outlet month over month), faster (one pass instead of waiting for the slowest of five calls) and cheaper. He's careful about scope: a specialist wins at one narrow job done millions of times, not at everything. A monthly loop of sampling, expert review, retraining and benchmarking keeps it from missing next year's euphemisms. His closing line for any team: ship the loop, not the model.

Who should watch

Teams paying per-call LLM bills for a narrow classification task, anyone designing a labelling pipeline with LLMs and humans together, and people working on trust and safety or media tooling. The talk shares no exact cost or latency figures, so come for the architecture rather than benchmarks.

entry.title: In real-time bidding, a late answer is a no answer
entry.summary: Sujan Challa (Samsung Electronics America) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on building an ad auction platform around a 100 ms latency wall.
entry.content:
When the exchange closes the auction at about 100 milliseconds, a slow bid simply doesn't count. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, Sujan Challa, Senior Software Engineer at Samsung Electronics America working on connected-TV advertising, walked through a real-time bidding architecture built one forced move at a time, each move dictated by that deadline.

His framing is the useful part: treat the latency budget as an architectural constraint, not a performance target, and let it decide where state lives, what waits on what, and what gets dropped.

Every synchronous hop is a purchase

The naive design (request in, database lookup, bid out) dies on contact. A database call per request multiplies load, and one slow dependency sets the floor for the whole system. Sujan's three opening moves:

  1. Feature cache in front of everything. User context, campaign and model inputs come from memory. The price is staleness, so expiry, invalidation and source-of-truth recovery are designed up front. Strict consistency is reserved for facts that need it, like budget accounting.
  2. Parallelise the independent waits. The bidder fans out to user, budget and model lookups at once; the slowest bounded call sets the join time, not the sum.
  3. Scale replicas, not state. Any healthy stateless bidder can serve any request, so capacity is more replicas in more regions, not a redesign.

His one-line generalisation: under a strict budget, every synchronous hop is paid for in milliseconds, and precomputation plus locality is how you stop paying retail.

The pod is the unit of correctness

Connected TV adds a wrinkle the web never had: ads arrive in pods, several impressions in one commercial break that must be decided together. Two car ads back-to-back, or the same ad twice in a break, is a failure even when every single auction was correct.

The auction core only understands single impressions. Rather than fork it, the platform decomposes each pod into plain impressions, runs them through the core, and reassembles at the edge, where deal tiers, competitive separation and frequency rules live. Frequency state spans requests, so it sits in shared state at that edge layer. The pattern to steal: rules that span requests belong at the layer that can see the whole unit of work. Push them into the core and the core stops being boring and reusable.

Degradation is a feature with an owner

The live path has a failure table, and it's a real design document rather than an apology. Cache miss: read the source, repopulate. Slow lookup: use a safe default and continue. Repeated failures: open the circuit. Deadline exhausted: return no bid rather than a late one. Timeouts are a design input; a missing signal is cheaper than a missed auction.

Everything not needed to answer moves off the path. Win, loss and impression events go through pub/sub into logging, billing and training data; models retrain offline and refresh the serving layer. The learning loop improves the live path without standing in it. Observability gets the same treatment: P95, P99 and P999 are the product metrics, but measuring costs budget too, so telemetry is sampled, aggregated at the edge and shipped asynchronously. The live path emits; it never waits to report.

Who should watch

Anyone running payments, search, recommendations or anything else with a hard latency wall; Sujan's point is that they all converge on the same moves. It's an architecture talk with no code, so it suits tech leads and architects more than someone after a Go profiling session. If your services have timeouts but no defaults, the four closing lessons alone are worth the time.
