entry.title: Conf42 Feature Flags 2026: kill switches, migrations and model gates
entry.summary: Conf42 Feature Flags 2026 roundup: 16 talks from Harness, Capital One, Adobe, Bank of America, Confluent and more on flags for AI agents, migrations and models.
entry.content:
The first Conf42 Feature Flags conference ran on October 15, 2026, under the tagline Flip features, not tables!, and it quickly became clear that nobody on the lineup thinks of a flag as a boolean any more. Across 16 talks, engineers from Harness, Capital One, Walmart, Adobe, Bank of America, Confluent, PayPal and Amazon used flags as kill switches for AI agents, routers for migrations, gates for model releases and runtime controls for production diagnostics. Everything is on the event page.

Four themes carried the day.

A flag stops new work, not running work

The most memorable opening of the event belonged to Parthiban Rajasekaran of Capital One, in "Your AI Kill Switch Is Probably Broken". In a simulated drill he disables an agent, the dashboard turns red, and a new request is rejected a second later. Fifteen seconds after that, a job that was already queued sends a customer email anyway. His point: most feature flags are admission controls, and a real kill switch for autonomous systems also needs cancellation semantics for work that's already in flight.

The rest of the agents track built on the same worry. Girish Konda of Microsoft, tech lead for capacity management in Microsoft Fabric, talked about a year of running agents against his real job (incident triage, telemetry, code review, runbooks) and the failure modes demos never show, like numbers with no source and citations to documents that don't exist. Pavan Boppidi of Walmart presented confidence-gated human-in-the-loop routing for autonomous logistics, with flags deciding how much autonomy each decision gets. And Ishan Shah of PayPal treated flag changes as incident evidence in Beacon, a governed workflow for AI-assisted root cause analysis that puts an explicit operator decision between hypothesis and action.

Migrations as a series of reversible steps

Harness's keynote set the frame. Ryan Vila walked through the strangler fig pattern with a flag doing the routing, a ramp from internal users to general availability, and the advice to step back a stage instead of killing a rollout. His closing section on flag hygiene (stale flags, untested defaults, drift between environments, clear ownership) is the part to share with your team.

Two talks applied that thinking to heavy, regulated systems. Jaya Chand Bandi showed flags as the engine for domain-driven decomposition of monolithic payment platforms, carving out business capabilities one at a time. Jaymin Sutarwala of United Therapeutics described retiring a legacy patient CRM for a Salesforce stack spanning Marketing Cloud, Data Cloud and Health Cloud, with identity resolution, segmentation and activation each gated behind flags because a big-bang cutover wasn't an option with patient data involved.

Pratham Yadav of the College of Southern Nevada raised a migration most teams forget: the one in the analytics layer. When a flagged change alters the logic behind a KPI, dashboards and executive reports change too, so he argued for metric versioning and reconciliation against the old definition before switching.

Gating models on quality, not just exposure

A flag decides who sees a feature. Three speakers asked what else it should check before widening. Pavan Rupanguntla of Bank of America separated model deployment from model activation for machine learning credit decisions, so a credit line strategy can ship dark and be released gradually with regulatory risk in mind.

Rajesh Lingam of Adobe pointed out that a GenAI feature can be technically healthy while its answers get less accurate, grounded or safe. His answer is continuous automated evaluation feeding quality gates that inform rollout decisions. And Rakshay Pawar of Codeflow Capital asked whether guardrail metrics stay valid when targeting changes mid-rollout, stress-testing static, rolling and adaptive conformal bounds on decades of U.S. Treasury yield data. Probably the only feature flag talk this year with a bond market in it.

Flags as runtime controls for operations

The reliability track used flags for things no product manager will ever see. Fuad Laguda, an independent engineer in Stirling who runs two production apps alone, keeps his diagnostics behind a Cloudflare KV flag with three states (off, admin only, everyone), because shipping a build with extra logging at 11pm is too slow and leaving detailed traces on all the time would store users' personal data. The same flag shape reports when his app fails over to a second language-model provider after four consecutive failures, and he forced that failover in production on purpose to prove it works.

At the other end of the scale, Naveen Goel of Amazon made the case for AI as an operator inside the SDLC for a connected-device fleet serving more than 200,000 requests per second, with performance-aware review, payload replay in CI and phased canary, cell and region rollouts. Prateek Jindal of Confluent covered self-healing cloud infrastructure, using flags to limit blast radius and disable unstable behaviour automatically. Anil Kumar of Allstate combined API health monitoring and auto-healing with flag-driven traffic controls, and Emmanuela Opurum of SoftNet Technologies gave an accessible tour of progressive rollouts, canaries and the common mistakes teams make with flags.

Sponsors

Thanks to Harness and SREday, the diamond sponsors of the event, and to HockeyStick for the podcast partnership.

What's next

Every talk is linked from the Conf42 Feature Flags 2026 page. The second edition, Conf42 Feature Flags 2027, is scheduled for June 24, 2027. If your kill switch has never been tested with work in flight, you have until then.

entry.title: Debezium Platform turns CDC from a ticket queue into self-service
entry.summary: Vincenzo Santonastaso (IBM, Debezium maintainer) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on scaling change data capture across teams with Debezium Platform.
entry.content:
The first change data capture pipeline is a win. The twentieth is a queue of tickets in front of the platform team. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, Vincenzo Santonastaso, Senior Software Engineer at IBM and a core maintainer of Debezium, argued that once CDC is popular, the hard part stops being CDC and becomes everything around it, and showed how Debezium Platform moves that work to self-service.

Honest scope up front: this is a talk by a Debezium maintainer about Debezium's own platform, with a live demo. It's open source, and the pitch is about operating model as much as tooling.

Why one team ends up owning everyone's pipelines

Vincenzo starts with a quick baseline (batch vs streaming, Lambda architecture, the streamhouse) and lands on log-based CDC: read the database's transaction log (binlog, WAL, redo log) instead of re-scanning tables, so you ship only the rows that changed with little load on the source. Debezium does this across MySQL, Postgres, Oracle, SQL Server, MongoDB, Db2, Cassandra and more, with one event format and offsets that let a restart resume exactly where it left off.

Then the catch. Shipping even one pipeline means knowing snapshots, offsets, schema changes, replication slots, permissions, dozens of connector properties, converters and SMTs, plus deployment, monitoring and upgrades. Nobody wants every product team to learn that, so the knowledge concentrates in the platform team. That works, until every team that wants a pipeline routes through the same few people who review configs, deploy connectors and answer tickets. The people waiting get slower; the platform team gets tired.

Raise the abstraction, keep the knobs

Debezium Platform's answer is to stop passing around raw connector JSON. The platform team defines reusable building blocks: sources, destinations and transformations. A pipeline is a combination of those, with room left for tuning. In Vincenzo's words, that is what turns a pile of configuration into a product.

The roles shift with it. Platform engineers own the building blocks and the guardrails. Data engineers create and manage their own pipelines from the UI or the CLI. The platform deploys and runs them and shows health, status, logs and metrics for every pipeline in one console, rather than everybody grepping logs across clusters.

The demo: one database, three very different consumers

The demo is the bit worth the watch. One Postgres inventory database, three teams:

  • Analytics wants clean rows upserted into a separate warehouse database via JDBC.
  • Integration wants row-change events pushed to an external HTTP endpoint as webhooks.
  • A third team wants current product and stock state in Redis.

Each pipeline gets its own replication slot, so they're independent. Under the hood: Debezium Platform installed with Helm on a local Kind cluster, a UI called Stage, a control plane and REST API called Conductor, and the Debezium operator, which deploys a dedicated Debezium Server pod per pipeline. There's no Kafka or Kafka Connect anywhere in the demo, which will surprise anyone who thinks of Debezium as a Kafka Connect plugin. Metrics flow through an OpenTelemetry Collector into Prometheus and back into the UI's dashboards.

Vincenzo builds the three pipelines in a few clicks, shows that every connector property in the forms carries its documentation inline, and then checks the webhook receiver, Redis and the warehouse tables. All three got their data. Demo gods appeased.

Who should watch

Platform teams already running Debezium on Kafka Connect who have become the CDC help desk, and data platform leads deciding how to offer CDC to many teams without a ticket per pipeline. If you've never touched CDC, the first third is a decent primer. If you want deep internals on snapshotting or schema evolution, this stays at the operating-model level.

entry.title: Feature flags turn a migration into a ramp you can walk back down
entry.summary: Ryan Vila of Harness at Conf42 Feature Flags 2026 on gradual, measurable, reversible cloud-native migrations, and the flag hygiene that keeps them safe.
entry.content:
A migration that can only move forward is a bet, not a plan. At Conf42 Feature Flags 2026, Ryan Vila, Americas Advisory Director at Harness, showed how feature flags turn a cloud-native migration into a series of small, measured steps, each of which you can pause or undo, and why the flags themselves need the same discipline as the code they guard.

Ryan works with teams adopting feature management and experimentation, and he came to Harness through Split, the feature management company Harness acquired. The talk is a vendor keynote, but most of it is practice you can apply with any flagging tool.

Three ways a migration goes wrong

Ryan opens with the failure modes he sees most often. The first is the big bang cutover: deployment and release are the same event, and teams often bundle a UI change, a pipeline change and a new service into one switch. If any one of them breaks, all of them roll back together, assuming they can.

The second is a forward-only path. If you can't pause halfway or step back a stage, nobody wants to start, and the migration stalls in planning. The third is an uncontrolled blast radius: when deploy equals release, 100% of users meet the bug at the same moment.

His answer is the strangler fig pattern, which he openly calls a refresher. Run the new service next to the old one, route a controlled slice of traffic to it with a flag, compare the two streams, and retire the old path once the evidence says so. Nothing new in the idea; the hard part is doing it on purpose.

Back up a stage instead of pulling the plug

The most useful part of the talk is the ramp. Ryan describes it as a ladder: internal users first, then test accounts with synthetic traffic or trusted customer QA teams, then a small release, then a measured ramp to general availability. What counts as small is up to you: 1% of traffic, one zip code, one region. The rule is the smallest blast radius that still lets you see a negative effect.

He asks you to treat the whole ramp like a load test. Something can be fine at 5% and break at 6%, so you keep measuring at every step, with the same metrics you used at the start.

The point people skip: when a metric goes wrong, the right move often isn't the kill switch. You can drop from the measured ramp back to the small release, or from the small release back to test accounts, learn what scale exposed, and climb again. Killing everything is sometimes more disruptive than stepping down one rung.

The flag is code, so test every state

Ryan closes with a cautionary section that deserves its own poster. Stale flags need a lifecycle and governance, because a forgotten flag is a landmine for whoever toggles it next while trying to work out what it does. Flags have more than on and off: there is a default state for when evaluation fails, and teams must test that fallback path too.

He also warns about configuration drift. Flag definitions in staging should match production, and if you keep flags in a disaster recovery environment, they should match production at the moment you fail over, or be off. And ownership has to be explicit, because whoever owns the flag owns the decision to flip it during an incident.

His summary line is the one to keep: the flag itself is a change. "It is its own code and therefore should be tested as code in all of its states." Then it gets deleted when nothing calls it any more, like any other dead code.

Three questions to take back to your team

The talk ends with homework for whatever migration you have in flight. How are you gating the new path, and is every element that changes actually behind a control? If it goes wrong, which flag reverts or scales back, and could that be automated instead of waiting for whoever is awake at 3am? And what is your rollback SLA, the time between "we have a problem" and solid ground again?

Who should watch

Platform and release engineers planning a re-platforming, and SREs who get asked to approve one. If your migration plan has a single cutover weekend on it, this one is worth your evening. If your team already runs progressive delivery with per-cohort metrics, the hygiene section is the part to send to everyone else.

entry.title: From prompt to product starts long before the first prompt
entry.summary: LaShawnda Rodgers (RGLC) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026 on taking an app from Reddit research and a PRD through AI builders to launch.
entry.content:
"Can you build me an app?" is, according to LaShawnda Rodgers, the wrong way to get an app built. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026, LaShawnda, founder of RGLC and an AI strategist, walked through the process she uses to take an idea to a launched product with AI builders, and most of the work she describes happens before anyone types a prompt.

It's a founder's playbook more than an engineering deep-cut: research, a requirements document, a builder choice, prompting, security, integrations and launch, illustrated with apps she built herself, one for parents in the middle of potty training and one that helps seniors and their caregivers make sense of the letters they receive.

Validate the problem where people complain

Her research stack is refreshingly low-tech. LinkedIn polls asking what people wish their favourite app did better. Reddit threads where people vent. Google Trends to see whether a pain point has search volume behind it; for potty training it did, down to long-tail questions about ages and diets. Facebook groups and local parenting groups, where she mostly listens. Perplexity for research with cited sources she can check.

Only once the demand looks real does she write anything down.

The PRD is the prompt's ancestor

The step she pushes hardest is a living product requirements document: the problem, the target user, the pain points from app store reviews and Reddit, competitors, pricing, the minimum features, the integrations needed, and how success gets measured. She splits features into phases, phase one being the smallest thing that can test the market, and keeps a "nice to have" list so that, say, voice doesn't sneak into an app that works without it.

That document then feeds the build. It's also the reference she checks the AI's output against, which is where the prompt engineering part of the title earns its place.

Prompts as specifications

Her prompting advice follows the familiar shape, but the examples are concrete: give the model a role (a senior full-stack product architect with accessibility expertise, rather than a one-line request to build an app for seniors), clear and short instructions, one or two examples, and enough context. Too many instructions, she warns, and the model starts to hallucinate.

Then she argues with it. She plays models against each other ("Gemini said this"), asks one to argue like an attorney for its choice, and asks it to rewrite her prompt. Her checking routine runs under the acronym SCOPE: specify what the product must and must not do, check every proposed feature against the agreed requirements, and watch for functionality the tool invented on its own, especially anything that will quietly cost tokens or money. Then inspect the code, and get someone independent to look at it.

Pick the builder like a vendor, not a trend

She builds on Emergent and Anything rather than whatever is trending, and shares her decision criteria: integrations (APIs, MCP, connectors), data ownership, whether you can reach a human at support without the most expensive plan, ease of maintenance, and cost per iteration in tokens and credits.

The security section is the part many "I built an app with AI" talks skip. Her apps use server-side auth on every API call (a 401 if you're not logged in), secrets kept out of the client, email verification tokens, rate limits on AI endpoints so nobody abuses them, audit logs, a retention policy that purges old logs, and account deletion with GDPR and CCPA in mind.

Integrations that make the app feel human

The demos lean on Resend for email and newsletters with delivery metrics, Telnyx for voice, SMS and toll-free numbers, and OpenAI Realtime for voice conversations. The best moment is the seniors' app: asked by voice about an appointment deadline in a Medicare letter, it replies that the letter is about plan changes and that the only deadline it mentions is the last day to switch plans. It answers what the letter says instead of inventing the deadline the question assumed.

Launch advice closes the talk: soft launch to friends, then Product Hunt, F6S, X, LinkedIn and Reddit, and treat feedback as the next phase of the PRD.

Who should watch

Builders and aspiring founders using AI app builders who want a repeatable process from idea to launch, and anyone who wants a checklist for the boring parts (requirements, auth, secrets) that demos usually leave out. Engineers looking for internals of the builders themselves can skip it; this is about process and judgment.

entry.title: BetBoom's own Dota 2 draft feed took conversion from 8.4% to 31.2%
entry.summary: Egor Kolovertnykh of BetBoom at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on turning Dota 2 Game State Integration snapshots into a live draft feed.
entry.content:
A live widget that runs five minutes behind the game is a history lesson, not a live widget. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, Egor Kolovertnykh, Senior Backend Developer at BetBoom, showed how his team stopped waiting on an external data provider for Dota 2 pick-and-ban updates and built their own source straight from the game client, in Go and Postgres, in about six weeks.

The payoff he reported is the kind product managers frame and hang on the wall: the widget fed by the in-house source got more than five million views during 2024, and its conversion rate was 31.2% against 8.4% for the partner-fed one.

The data source is a person running Dota

Dota 2 has a feature called Game State Integration (GSI). Drop a config file into the game folder with your endpoint, and the client POSTs its current state as JSON, picks and bans included. So BetBoom's "telemetry platform" starts on an operator's computer: someone joins the match, the game talks, the backend listens.

That framing matters for the rest of the talk. Half the engineering is about the human in the loop. Configs ship with a signed JWT carrying BetBoom's event ID and config ID, because the Dota game ID doesn't exist yet when the operator prepares the file. One config covers a whole series of maps. A new config starts in test mode: the operator opens a replay of any match, the service confirms picks and bans arrive, and only then does the config go live. The replay's game ID is kept aside so yesterday's heroes never show up on today's match page.

Snapshots are state; users want events

GSI doesn't send "team A banned Pudge". It sends the whole current board: pick and ban slots per team, filling up as the draft goes, with every earlier choice repeated in every request. Ten identical snapshots must produce the same widget, not ten new events.

Egor's fix was to encode the draft rules as an ordered list of steps (which side, pick or ban, which slot), infer which team went first by checking which ordering fits the observed slots, and then merge each snapshot into one array of actions. Known actions stay in place; new filled slots append. A neat side effect: if the operator joins late, the first snapshot already contains the earlier picks, so the draft can be rebuilt from it with no special catch-up path. State lived in a Go map behind a mutex, one entry per game, with configs and event links in Postgres.

Then production taught the usual lesson. Dota has both Captain's Mode and Captain's Draft, with different action orders, and to the backend they look nearly identical. The draft type went into the config, chosen by the operator. As Egor put it, when you work with a game you eventually have to check which rules the other side is playing by today.

Keep the old contract, win on priority

The part platform engineers should steal: the new service spoke the exact contract the platform already used for partner data. Teams, ordered actions, widget state. To everything downstream it was just another source. New draft modes stayed inside Egor's backend; nothing else had to learn Dota rules.

That made rollout gradual. At first a source was chosen per event; later the in-house data became the first choice, with the partner feed as fallback when it wasn't available. No big-bang migration of every match page, and the partner contract stayed alive.

Replays as a test harness

Replays did double duty in development. Change the code, reopen the same game, watch the draft again, compare. No waiting for the next tournament. Front-end developers and QA sat with the game on one screen and the website on the other, checking right hero, right team, right position, pick or ban. Watching Dota officially became part of the job, which is the most enviable acceptance-test setup at this conference.

Who should watch

Anyone building a real-time pipeline from a source that only gives you snapshots: game telemetry, IoT devices, polling APIs. It's also a tidy case study in replacing a vendor feed without breaking the consumers of it. If you want deep Kafka or scale numbers, this isn't that talk; it's a focused, honest build story.

entry.title: A customer-facing agent got reliable outside its prompt
entry.summary: Nowlun's Ahmed Gaber and Ahmed Morsi at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026 on clean data, code-held rules and staged evals for a freight sales copilot.
entry.content:
The copilot said there was no price for a 40-foot container from Shanghai to Jebel Ali, opened a request to the pricing team, and 35 minutes later a human quoted a rate the system already had. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026, Ahmed Gaber, Director of Product Engineering, and Ahmed Morsi, Product Engineer, both at freight platform Nowlun, walked through a year of running an AI copilot beside their sales team, and why most of its reliability came from the data and the system around the prompt.

The recording is presented by Ahmed Morsi. The short version, in his words: get the data right, build the system, and measure every change.

The setup: a copilot, not an autopilot

Nowlun customers compare, book and track sea and air freight, and every shipment starts with questions: the price to Jeddah, a Monday booking, a missing container. The copilot reads the ask, searches prices and quotes, drafts the reply and fills in the CRM. A sales rep sends, edits or picks up the phone. When the copilot can't help, it steps back with a reason from a fixed list.

Part one: the data was the bug

That missing Shanghai price existed three times, saved under different aliases for the port. It happened more than two hundred times in a month. The fix was "one thing, one ID": every spelling becomes an alias on one record, so 14 spellings map to one port code. Don't list spellings in the prompt, he warns; the list is never complete and costs tokens every turn. Searches that missed an existing price dropped from 30% to 4%.

The second habit is that field descriptions are prompts. More than a quarter of their fields had nobody who could say what they meant, so the team wrote a dictionary. The entry for the "comparing" stage now reads "Collecting quotes, not ready to book. Offer to hold the price. Don't push a booking." That sentence lives with the field and travels into tool descriptions and onboarding. Tool calls with a wrong argument fell from 18% to 5%. Before touching the prompt, pricing requests for prices they already had went from more than two hundred a month to thirty, and finding the right price went from eleven minutes to forty seconds.

Part two: rules live in code when they're costly and checkable

They wrote the search-first rule into the prompt in capitals, and the copilot still opened requests without searching. So the rule moved into the request tool: no search, no request, and the refusal says what to do instead.

Ahmed describes code versus prompt as a dial. Far left, code hides tools until the stage allows them or enforces a sequence. In the middle sits what they call refuse then check: an LLM judge reviews a stated reason, and after two refusals the call goes through, so a wrong judge can't leave the copilot stuck. Further right, hints in tool results. Far right, judgment left to the model.

Writes get stricter checks than words. A hallucinated "we ship coal" saved to the CRM marked a lead as a prohibited commodity, set it to lost and stopped all follow-ups. Now every write tool must carry a sourced quote from the conversation, fuzzy-matched against the thread.

Their 500-plus line prompt turned out to be nine places that never saw each other, holding 70 rules and 24 conflicts. A nine-question decision list now gives each instruction one home, and only rules that hold on every turn in every stage reach the base prompt. On 44 scripted conversations with the same model, passing went from 55% with one big prompt to 70% when split by owner, and to 80% once the conflicts were settled.

Part three: measure every change

A price search refactor silently dropped the expiry filter; a pricing analyst noticed days later. After that, every change got measured. Step-backs caused by the copilot itself fell from 46% in Q2 to 1% in Q4, leaving the rest as real sales work. Tests are recorded at the first stage they fail, an idea he credits to a talk featuring Hamel Husain on failure funnels, and graded on what the copilot did, what the system actually saved and what it said.

Two stories stand out. Tone: suggestions were about fifteen times longer than reps' typical WhatsApp replies, because the tone rewriter never saw the conversation. And the rare coal-style fabrication showed up 2 times in 1,000 replays at temperature 1, too rare to prove a fix, so they replayed at 1.5 to get 15 in 1,000, then drove it to zero with the source-quote parameter.

Who should watch

Anyone running an agent that talks to customers or writes to a CRM. It's long and packed with real numbers, and the closing checklist (one ID per thing, code what's costly and checkable, one home per instruction, staged evals, hot replays) is directly usable.

entry.title: Treat tokens like money: a GenAI gateway with budget holds
entry.summary: Brindal Patel of Coinbase at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on a GenAI gateway with card-style token budgets, safe semantic caching and eval-gated failover.
entry.content:
A background service hits a timeout, enters a fast retry loop, and every retry calls an expensive foundation model with a shared API key pasted into a config file. By morning the bill is enormous, nobody can tell which service did it, and revoking the key breaks production for every other team. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, Brindal Patel, a senior software engineer at Coinbase, called that a missing platform contract, not an AI problem, and laid out the gateway that supplies one.

He's clear at the start that the talk is based on his own experience and independent work, not affiliated with or endorsed by his employer.

The paved road is one YAML file

The product contract is small. A team opens one pull request with a short YAML file and gets back a model alias (no vendor SDK, no key in the repo), a budget with a named owner, and a distributed trace for every call. That replaces the N-times-M mess of every team wiring every provider: scattered keys, no owner for spend, uncoordinated rate limits, and the same prompt paid for again and again.

A request passes six stages: mTLS and a token identify the calling team; an Envoy external-processing filter strips PII and secrets; Open Policy Agent decides; the gateway places a budget hold; a tenant-scoped cache gets a chance to answer; otherwise the call routes to a model and the bill settles. Each stage emits an OpenTelemetry span, and MCP tool calls go through the same door and the same policy.

Budget tokens like a card payment

The first idea is the one to steal. You don't know output cost until the model finishes, so ten parallel requests can all pass an under-budget check and overrun together. Brindal borrows from card payments: authorise a hold for the worst case (input tokens plus max output), capture only what the response reports, release the rest. For broken streams, cancel upstream, settle what was used, release the remainder. The check and the hold are one atomic step, so parallel calls can't spend the same budget twice.

Similar is not the same when money moves

The second idea is a warning about semantic caching. "Send one hundred dollars to my savings" and "send one thousand" look almost identical to an embedding model. After PII redaction, everyone's balance question looks like the same text. So before serving a cached answer the gateway checks four things: same scope (tenant, model, system prompt, decoding settings), similarity above a threshold tuned per model, matching entities compared by hash so raw account numbers are never stored, and whether this prompt should be cached at all. Transactional and per-user prompts never are.

He frames caching as a ladder you climb only as far as your checks allow: provider prompt caching for shared prefixes, then exact-match, then semantic behind the four checks, and for self-hosted models, KV-cache-aware routing to GPU workers whose prefixes are already warm.

Fail over only to models that passed your evals

The third idea: an untested backup might ignore your JSON schema or answer worse. Evals run in CI on every model change, and the runtime router only reads an in-memory passed flag. On a 500, timeout or 429, it walks the tenant's approved list, skips anything that didn't pass that tenant's evals, tags the span as a failover, and returns a clear error if nothing is left. Never a silent downgrade.

The policy itself is shown as Rego for OPA 1.x: default deny, allow only if the model is on the tenant's lease, the data scan is clean and the hold fits, with an optional degrade to a smaller internal model. Allow and degrade can never both match.

Practical edges

The tracing tips are concrete: name model spans the OpenTelemetry way, keep gateway infrastructure on the resource and the calling tenant on each request span for chargeback, and pin your schema version because the GenAI conventions are still in development. His four review-time mistakes are worth a sticky note: shared caches across tenants, budget checks after the call, failover to any model that answers, and embedding prompts before redaction.

Who should watch

Platform teams turning ad-hoc LLM usage into a shared service, and anyone who has had to explain a surprise model bill. It's short and dense with patterns; his advice is to start with quick wins and avoid writing a gateway from scratch.

entry.title: Pack five metrics into one LLM judge call, but not forty
entry.summary: Scarlett Attensil of LaunchDarkly at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on how many criteria one LLM judge can score before accuracy slips.
entry.content:
Scoring five metrics in one LLM judge call instead of five separate calls cut Scarlett Attensil's evaluation bill by 46% with no measurable loss in accuracy. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, Scarlett, a developer educator at LaunchDarkly and a former data scientist, showed the experiment behind that number, and the second one that found the judge slowly getting worse as the list grows toward 40.

If your platform team runs a shared eval service, this is the most directly useful half hour of the event.

Where the savings actually come from

Her judge returned evidence, a short reason and a score for every metric. Sent one metric per call, it read the same response five times and reasoned five times. Packed, it reads once and fills out a checklist. Prompt caching helps with the repeated input, she notes, but it can't touch the model's reasoning tokens, and those were the bigger saving.

From her billing records: about 1,000 metric scores cost 59 cents unpacked and about 32 cents packed. The abstract gives the precise figures, $0.593 versus $0.318 per thousand criteria.

Same prompt, both ways

The first experiment used NVIDIA's public HelpSteer2 dataset, where humans scored responses from zero to four on helpfulness, correctness, coherence, complexity and verbosity. For roughly 150 prompts with a clear human preference, the judge scored both responses, and a match meant it ranked them in the same order as people, even if its numbers were a point harsher.

Everything stayed fixed except packing: same prompts, model and rubric wording, metric order shuffled with a recorded seed, and the output budget grown by the same 220 tokens per metric so a big call never ran out of room. Each prompt was scored both ways, so it served as its own control. Result: the confidence interval ran from about three points worse to four points better and crossed zero. No measurable change.

She also tracked ties, which most people forget. The judge tied about 48% of the time in both setups. If packing had pushed hard cases into ties, accuracy would look fine only because the hard ones dropped out. Her advice: always report the tie rate next to accuracy.

Breaking answers on purpose

HelpSteer2 has human labels for only five attributes, so to test 10, 20 and 40 metrics she built synthetic corruptions with a known right answer: filler phrases, broken grammar, repeated sentences, shuffled order, truncated endings, a deleted key sentence, wrong numbers. The haiku about a banana that now opens with a line of bureaucratic throat-clearing is a highlight. Each edit targets one metric and declares the direction the score should move.

The measured metric always sat first, and extra metrics piled up behind it, so position couldn't explain any drop.

A slow bend, not a cliff

At 40 metrics, across more than 7,000 calls, the judge caught the planted change about six points less often, with the whole interval on the negative side. There was no cliff. Every added metric cost roughly 1% in the odds of catching the change, a slow bend you'd miss if you were waiting for something to fall over.

The breakdown is the interesting part. Repetition suffered most: caught about two-thirds of the time with one metric, under a third with 40. Grammar and punctuation also slipped. Truncation and wrong numbers got easier to catch, possibly because extra metrics like completeness nudged the judge to check those.

What to do on Monday

Start with a small packed rubric; five worked and nearly halved her bill. Retest whenever the rubric grows, look at each metric on its own rather than the average, run detail-oriented metrics like tone and grammar as their own calls, define every point on your scale, and report ties. Her caveats are explicit: one model, one dataset, one rubric. The method is what transfers, and the repo with data, code and calls is linked from the talk.

Who should watch

Anyone running LLM-as-judge in CI or production, and platform teams pricing a shared evaluation service. It's also a tidy lesson in paired experimental design.

entry.title: Code Mode cut an MCP agent's tool context from 150K to 22K tokens
entry.summary: Adobe's Nishant Kumar Thakur and Sonam Raj at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026 on typed tool stubs for MCP, what they saved and where they broke.
entry.content:
Adobe's production agent was burning 150K tokens on tool definitions before the user typed a word, and picking the right tool only 42% of the time. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026, Nishant Kumar Thakur, Senior Computer Scientist, and Sonam Raj, Computer Scientist, both at Adobe, showed how switching to Code Mode (typed API stubs the model reads like library code) took that to 22K tokens and 80% tool-selection accuracy, then spent a refreshing amount of time on what went wrong.

Same tools, different presentation. That's the whole trick, and the details are where it gets interesting.

The fixed context tax

Their agent connects to everyday developer tools: Outlook, SharePoint, Jira, Confluence, Slack and a few others. Connect them all through plain MCP schemas and 75% of a 200K context window is gone before anyone says hello. The talk opens with an even bigger number from Cloudflare: describing 2,594 tools took about 1.17 million tokens, nearly six times a 200K window.

The second cost is less obvious. Ask the agent to attach a meeting transcript from Google Drive to a Salesforce lead, and the transcript enters the context on the read, then gets written out again as an argument on the update. You're paying a frontier model to copy and paste.

The third is accuracy. When nearly every service has a search, get and list operation with similar names, the model gets confused. That 42% doesn't show up on your token bill, but it shows up everywhere else.

Let the model write code against a typed API

The idea, credited to Cloudflare's Code Mode and a similar Anthropic write-up: models have seen far more real code than tool-call JSON, so give them a typed API and let them write a script. The script runs in a sandbox, intermediate data stays in variables, and only the result returns to the model. Tool definitions load on demand through progressive disclosure, so the model explores the available tools like a developer browsing a code base.

On their production agent, with the same tasks and model, prompt tokens before the user's question went from 150K to 22K, an 85% reduction. Tool-selection accuracy went from 42% to 80%. Their explanation is that the model sees fewer similar tools at once and focuses on the typed definitions it needs.

The demo didn't hit the headline number

The live demo uses Pi, an open source terminal coding agent with Code Mode built in, against dummy Jira, Confluence and Slack MCP servers with 86 tools. With direct tool calls, tool definitions alone took 54K tokens, and one task (review five Jira bugs and two runbooks, post a summary to Slack) reached about 98K. With Code Mode the session started at 1.2K tokens, and the same task landed around 34K: a 65% reduction, "but not quite what we expected", as they put it.

The reason is instructive. One well-behaved script made five MCP calls in parallel, picked only the needed fields and trimmed descriptions to 400 characters. Others returned full Jira issues and complete search results. Code Mode removes the upfront schemas; it doesn't control what comes back.

Five ways it broke

Nishant's honest section lists the failure modes. The model called methods that didn't exist, so the sandbox returns the closest match and they treat it as a retry. MCP servers changed and generated stubs went stale, so stubs are regenerated at connection time. One big types file per server recreated the schema dump in a new format; the fix was one file per tool. Output bloat needed an explicit instruction to return only necessary fields. And debugging got harder, so every tool call inside the sandbox is logged with arguments and result size.

They're also clear about when not to use it: agents with three tools, setups without a trusted sandbox, and workflows that need human approval at every step. In those cases tool search, which keeps normal tool calling but loads only relevant definitions, is the simpler option.

Who should watch

Anyone running an agent against more than a handful of MCP servers. The homework is cheap: log prompt tokens just before the user message is added, try Code Mode on one task, and compare with the same model. If that first number is already in the tens of thousands, you have a project.

entry.title: The feature store behind every For You feed, explained
entry.summary: Attila Toth of ScyllaDB at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on online feature stores, P99 tail latency, query-first data models and pluggable stores.
entry.content:
Every swipe on a For You feed is an event, and the next item you see depends on features fetched in a few milliseconds. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, Attila Toth, developer advocate at ScyllaDB and a contributor to the Feast feature store project, walked through the infrastructure behind those feeds: offline and online stores, why P99 rules everything, and how to model data so one request hits one partition.

It's a vendor talk in the honest sense. The examples come from ScyllaDB users like ShareChat and its short-video app Moj, Medium, Tripadvisor and Agoda, and the design advice holds whichever database you pick.

Two stores, two very different jobs

A feature is a signal the model uses to predict, attached to an entity: likes on a post in the last 10 minutes, shares in the last seven days. Attila's point is that you can invent endless variations (why 10 minutes and not 60?), so teams need one place to create, store and query them.

A feature store splits into an offline store for training, holding huge historical datasets, and an online store for real-time inference, serving a small feature vector per request under a strict latency SLA. He cites Tripadvisor at about 125 TB offline against 9 TB online in ScyllaDB. The organisational wins are reuse (one team's feature serves every model) and self-service: data scientists ship features without waiting on an engineering team.

The page is as fast as its slowest lookup

The best slide is the tail latency maths. One user action fans out to many API calls and many database reads, and the page waits for the slowest. If a page does 100 lookups and each beats P99 with 99% probability, the chance all 100 are fast is 0.99 to the power 100, so about 63% of page loads wait for at least one slow lookup. That's why online stores are judged on P99, and why Attila recommends the Google paper The Tail at Scale.

Design the table for the query

For low latency he flips relational habits. Start from the screen, write the queries it needs, then design one table per query, denormalising freely. Medium's published schema is his example: a narrow table with entity ID, feature key and value, so adding or dropping a feature never means a schema migration.

The primary key does the heavy lifting. Feature key plus entity ID form the composite partition key, so a query lands on exactly one partition. A clustering key sorted descending keeps the most recent items first on disk, so nothing gets re-sorted at read time.

He adds three more levers. Treat vector embeddings as features, stored in the same table with a vector index, instead of standing up a separate vector database. Use TTL so expired rows leave the hot store and history lives in cheaper storage like Parquet on S3. Pre-aggregate counts into time buckets with a stream processor such as Flink, as ShareChat does, instead of scanning raw events.

Cache layers and spiky bills

On caching, Attila is candid about his bias: an external cache like Redis or DAX in front of a database means two systems to pay for and run, and ScyllaDB's pitch is an embedded cache in a persistent database. On cost, he points to autoscaling against a target utilisation so a sporting-event spike doesn't mean paying for peak capacity all year.

Keep the online store pluggable

The Feast section ties it together. Feast keeps feature definitions in one place with one API, lets you plug in different offline stores (S3, Snowflake) and online stores (ScyllaDB, Redis, DynamoDB), and now supports vector search. His final takeaway is to keep the online store swappable: if it can't meet your P99, you want to change the database, not the whole architecture.

Who should watch

Platform and data engineers building recommendation or personalisation backends, and anyone who has watched a feed page stall on one slow read. The CQL examples are ScyllaDB and Cassandra flavoured; the reasoning travels.

entry.title: Single-layer LLM guardrails miss attacks spread across turns
entry.summary: Manvitha Potluri at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026 tested 390 prompts on AWS Bedrock; a second intent layer caught what keyword filters missed.
entry.content:
A keyword guardrail caught 43 of 190 prompt injection attacks in Manvitha Potluri's test set. Adding an independent semantic layer that reads the conversation caught 184, with zero false alarms on 200 legitimate prompts. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026, Manvitha, DevOps Cloud Solutions Architect at 24x7 Systems, showed why a single guardrail fails structurally, and confessed the evaluation mistake that nearly fooled her.

The talk is twenty minutes of measured results, which is rarer in guardrail talks than it should be.

The test set includes the boring prompts

Her set has 390 prompts: 172 single-turn attacks, 18 multi-turn sequences and 200 completely legitimate prompts. The legitimate ones matter because a guardrail that blocks everything has perfect detection and is useless. The attacks cover 15 categories drawn from the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications and wider taxonomies: instruction override, persona hijacking, encoding and obfuscation, multi-language, code injection, hypothetical framing, authority claims, incremental escalation and more. The threat model assumes an attacker who can see outputs, retry, and knows a filter exists.

Four detectors went through it. Keyword filtering detected 22.6% of attacks. A NeMo-style rule baseline managed about 21.6%. A perplexity detector did worst at 10%, because most attacks are written in perfectly ordinary language. The semantic intent classifier detected 96.8%, with an F1 of 0.984. Four of the 15 categories got past every rule-based system completely.

The attack lives in the trajectory

The multi-turn result is the one to remember. The keyword layer caught 5 of the 18 sequences; a classifier with conversation context caught all 18. Her example: write a training guide for a security tool, ask what attackers send to support bots, ask for one word for word, then ask the model to act on it. No single message contains an attack phrase.

She names three structural limits of a boundary filter: it reads one message, it reads only what users type (so indirect injection through retrieved documents, emails or tool output never reaches it), and it matches form rather than meaning. More keywords can't fix any of those.

Dual detection, deliberately simple

Layer one stays: AWS Bedrock Guardrails with content filtering, PII detection, denied topics and grounding checks, typically under a hundred milliseconds. Layer two runs only when layer one passes. It's a fast, low-cost model with a structured prompt that sees the current message plus up to five prior turns and returns JSON: risk level, attack type, confidence and a short reason. The primary model is only called if both pass.

Two design choices carry the pattern. The layers use different methods, so they fail differently. And the thing being attacked shouldn't also judge the attack, which is why the classifier isn't your main model. Every decision from both layers goes to an audit log in DynamoDB.

She treats false positives as a production failure too. Over-blocking frustrates users, prompts tickets to loosen the rules, and eventually someone builds a path around the guardrail. She chose the blocking threshold by sweeping five confidence levels rather than guessing, and notes that a coding assistant and a banking chatbot shouldn't share one.

The results file that was all throttling errors

The confession: during one Bedrock run, every prompt had a row and every row had a response. The responses were throttling exceptions. Depending on scoring, an error looks like a block (flattering) or a pass (unflattering), and either way the numbers look plausible. She caught it by reading raw samples, threw the results out, rebuilt the infrastructure and re-ran.

Her checklist is worth stealing: type every response (answered, blocked, errored) and never store them in one field; fail the run when errors exceed a small budget; read samples from every category before trusting a summary; always report false alarms next to detection.

Agents get five layers

For agents the worst outcome is an action, not text. Her five-layer Bedrock design adds tool authorisation (routine, destructive or denied), output and confidence checks, and a human approval gate for high-risk actions. On a separate evaluation on live AWS infrastructure she reported 94% accuracy, a 6% false positive rate, and latency of about 1.8 seconds against 13.9 seconds for the baseline. The dataset and code are open source under Apache 2.0, and the guardrail ships as a Terraform module.

Who should watch

Anyone with a guardrail in front of an LLM app or agent, and anyone who has written an eval harness. The throttling story alone justifies the twenty minutes.

entry.title: A correct diagnosis doesn't give an AI agent the authority to act
entry.summary: Ruby Agarwal, VP of Engineering at Avaya, at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on scoped, expiring authority for agents that remediate production.
entry.content:
An AI agent can be completely right about why production broke and still be wrong to fix it. That's the core of Ruby Agarwal's talk at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026. Ruby, Vice President of Engineering at Avaya, argues that self-service platforms were built to validate whether an action can run safely, and agents force a new question: should this agent be allowed to decide the action is needed at all?

2:14am, 96% confident, still not obviously safe

She opens on an incident bridge. A deployment went out eight minutes ago, p99 latency has jumped and error rates went from 1.8% to 7.4%. A monitoring agent correlates the deploy with metrics, traces and logs and recommends an immediate rollback with 96% confidence.

Then she adds context. The release included a database schema change. The previous version retried more aggressively. The service shares a database with other customer-facing apps. The diagnosis may be correct, but the rollback is suddenly not the obvious move, and that gap is the whole talk.

Later she plays the scenario forward: the rollback works, service A recovers, dashboards go green, and the old retry policy starts hammering the shared database until services B and C degrade. The problem has changed address. Local success isn't system success.

Decision, authority, execution

Ruby splits the platform contract into three parts. Decision: what the agent believes should happen and why. Authority: whether it has been delegated the right to make that decision under these conditions. Execution: whether the platform can safely perform the authorised action against current state. She doesn't want one agent diagnosing, granting itself authority, executing and declaring success.

Her model for authority is a short-lived lease, not a standing permission. An agent might be allowed to roll back one stateless service to a verified previous version, only with fresh evidence, a compatible state and no conflicting remediation running, and only for a limited time. As she puts it: "We're delegating a decision within boundaries. We're not handing an agent permanent control of production."

Propose, adjudicate, commit, verify

The architecture has four steps. The agent proposes a structured intent: service, current and target versions, evidence, expected customer impact and stop conditions. An independent authority service checks the agent's scope, evidence freshness, dependency health, blast radius and parallel remediations, then allows, denies or escalates. The executor revalidates right before acting, because time-of-check versus time-of-use bites here too. Then the platform verifies the customer outcome, since a successful rollback API call isn't proof of recovery. Every step lands in a decision record that explains why, not only what.

Her worked ending is a nice touch. The same 96% recommendation is allowed when evidence is fresh and the shared dependency healthy, escalated when the database's health is unknown, and denied when the evidence is 18 minutes old. Authority is evaluated in context, not stapled to an agent's identity.

Two reasonable agents can make an outage

One scenario every SRE will recognise: a release agent rolls back while a capacity agent scales, the scaling shifts traffic, the release agent reacts again, the capacity agent scales down. Each decision is reasonable; together they oscillate. Ruby's answer is the classic toolkit applied to agents: concurrency controls, resource ownership, fencing, cool-down periods, arbitration, and a way for the incident commander to take control.

Earn autonomy per decision class

Rollout goes observe, recommend, act within bounds, then act and report. Being great at detecting memory pressure doesn't earn the right to run database failovers, and authority narrows again when performance drops. She's also blunt about rubber-stamp approval buttons: a human clicking yes on dozens of recommendations isn't oversight. Accountability means owning the authority you delegated.

Who should watch

Platform engineers and SREs designing agent-driven remediation, and leaders deciding who owns those decisions. It's a framework talk without code, and the incident scenario makes every point land.

entry.title: A Claw is a coding agent that never logs off
entry.summary: Erik Hanchett of AWS at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on Claws, the always-on coding agents with memory, schedules, chat apps and sandboxes.
entry.content:
Erik Hanchett's coding agent reads the tech news every morning, writes a digest, and sends it to his Discord with an audio version he listens to while working out. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, Erik, Senior Developer Advocate at AWS, explained what turns a coding agent into a "Claw": an always-on assistant with memory, schedules and chat access that keeps working after you close the laptop.

It's an approachable introduction, half tour of the ecosystem and half demo of AWS's own open-source Claw, and Erik says up front that it's his opinionated short list.

Agent vs Claw

The distinction he draws is useful even if you never install one. A coding agent, in his framing, starts, does a task and ends: refactor this, fix that. A Claw is always running, usually on your own hardware or a server, with shell, browser, MCP and model access. It has memory of your preferences (the .NET developer gets .NET projects; the tabs-versus-spaces war is settled once), runs tasks on a schedule, talks to you over Slack, Telegram, Discord or text, and writes its own skill files as it learns.

You can still run narrow agents inside a Claw, for example a dedicated code reviewer with its own skills, tools and prompt.

Who's in the field

Erik names three he follows. OpenClaw is the most popular, self-hosted, with around four hundred thousand GitHub stars and a big skill hub. Hermes Agent from Nous Research has a learning loop that writes its own skills. The third is AWS's open-source dev workspace with sandboxing built in, which came out of internal use by AWS builders before it was open-sourced in August 2026 and can drive existing harnesses like Claude Code and Codex.

He doesn't skip the security history: early CVEs, and 824 malicious skills found in ClawHub. Things have settled since, he says, but you still need to be careful. He also notes consumer cousins like Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots that book and shop for you.

What people actually use them for

The demo section is where the talk gets concrete. A scheduler tab sets up cron-style jobs (his morning news run lives there). Triggers can hook into CI/CD, so a failed pipeline hits a webhook and the Claw summarises the failure for the right person. Internally at AWS, he describes a morning bug triage summary and a PR babysitter that reads review comments and replies.

A task runner takes a Markdown spec and keeps looping until the spec is satisfied. A trust mode lets a session run commands without prompting inside a sandbox, with deny rules alongside. Erik reaches his home-lab instance from his phone over Tailscale and SSH port forwarding, and once built an app that way while on vacation. Whether that sounds like freedom or a pager you can't put down is between you and your manager.

The rough edges, stated plainly

The closing caveats are the most useful slide for a platform team considering this. Prompt injection is still a problem. Long tasks still fail. Overnight jobs burn credits, so choose the model carefully. In a team setting you need governance, with policies the agent can't raise for itself and one policy for the fleet. And you're still responsible for reviewing what it produces.

His suggested first step is sensible: pick one boring daily chore, such as going through PRs, schedule it, keep the sandbox on and autopilot off.

Who should watch

Developers curious about always-on agents who want a fast map of the space, and platform teams who'll soon be asked whether engineers can run one at work. It's an intro and a product tour of an AWS project, not a deep security analysis; pair it with the hardening talks below.

entry.title: In anti-money laundering work, a prompt is a compliance control
entry.summary: Pratik Patel of Hexaware at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026 on grounded, schema-checked prompts for AML investigations that never infer intent.
entry.content:
"Explain why this transaction is suspicious" looks like a harmless prompt until you notice it has already decided the answer. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026, Pratik Patel, Principal Consultant at Hexaware Technologies, argued that in a bank a prompt is a control, and should be designed, tested and governed like any other control in an anti-money laundering (AML) workflow.

Pratik has spent more than 14 years on financial services transformation, with AML, fraud and cloud modernisation work for banks including TD Bank, Royal Bank of Canada and Santander. The talk reads like it: fewer clever tricks, more audit questions.

The leading prompt problem

The opening contrast is the best part. The basic prompt assumes suspicion and invites the model to build a story, and models are very good at building stories when evidence is thin. The governed version reads: "Summarize the supplied transaction evidence, identify documented alert indicators, cite supporting record IDs, and flag information gaps. Do not infer criminal intent."

The model summarises instead of concluding, cites record IDs, says what's missing and stays away from intent. Pratik distils it into five principles: context grounding, structured instructions, evidence traceability, controlled reasoning (facts separate from hypotheses) and safe failure.

Where AI sits in the pipeline

His workflow runs ingest, enrich, alert, summarise, investigate. The model helps in the last two steps only. It doesn't replace transaction monitoring and doesn't make the call. For Currency Transaction Reporting, which is rule-driven (in the US, cash over ten thousand dollars in a business day triggers a report), AI gathers related transactions and checks fields, and the analyst validates the aggregation.

The architecture is five layers: enterprise data sources, a governed cloud-native data platform, prompt orchestration, compliance applications, and governance drawn over all of them. His warning about layer two is worth repeating: if the data underneath is messy, the AI produces messy answers, only faster and more fluently.

Facts, indicators, assessments

The pyramid slide separates three kinds of statement that must never blur. Verified facts come straight from source systems. Observed indicators are patterns that warrant review against monitoring criteria. Investigative assessments are interpretations, reviewed and owned by an analyst, never determined by the model.

His contrast example: a weak output says the customer is structuring deposits to avoid reporting. A governed one lists five cash deposits between $9,000 and $9,900 across four days, with transaction references, and says the pattern warrants analyst review. Same facts, very different liability.

Valid JSON is not a true answer

Outputs follow a schema: case ID, transaction summary, indicators each with evidence IDs, missing information, and a review status that starts as pending analyst review, never approved. Four gates sit behind it: schema enforcement, evidence verification (if the model cites a transaction that was never retrieved, the output is rejected), completeness checks, and escalation to a correction workflow or an analyst.

The caution he underlines is the one most teams skip. A well-formed response tells you nothing about whether it's correct, which is why evidence checks and human review sit on top of schema validation.

Fail safe, and treat documents as data

Pratik lists failure scenarios with a control for each: request more evidence when it's missing, flag conflicting customer records, reject unsupported claims, block unauthorised access, retry bad formats within limits, and require human review when confidence is low. "In regulated operations, a safe refusal or escalation is always better than a confident, unsupported answer."

He also covers prompt injection in a case file (hidden text telling the model to mark the case low risk is data, never a command) and a flat ban on autonomous regulatory submissions. Governance means versioned prompts with approval gates, least-privilege access, and audit trails good enough to answer who approved this prompt, what data it saw and who reviewed the output.

Who should watch

Engineers and architects building LLM features in banking, insurance or any regulated review workflow. It's a framework talk without a live demo, and the rollout plan (start with bounded summarisation tasks, measure from day one) makes it a good brief to hand a compliance stakeholder.

entry.title: Agent engineering starts by assuming the model gets fooled
entry.summary: Cynthia Akiotu of Accenture at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on identity, MCP tools and authorization checks that hold when prompt injection works.
entry.content:
A customer asks a support agent about refunds, the agent retrieves the refund policy, and hidden in that document is an instruction to export every customer case to an outside address. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, Cynthia Akiotu, AI security and data protection architect at Accenture and a Microsoft MVP in Security Copilot, used that one scenario to argue that once an LLM can act, every engineering decision becomes a security decision.

Her design goal is refreshingly modest: don't pretend the model can't be manipulated. Contain what happens when it is.

Same model, new blast radius

Cynthia starts by putting prompt engineering and agent engineering side by side. The model is identical. What changed is everything around it: instructions, context, identity, tools, actions and governance. A chatbot that answers wrongly misleads someone. An agent that acts wrongly sends the email, updates the record or deletes it.

Each layer adds capability and widens the blast radius unless it's deliberately constrained. And these layers aren't one team's checklist; identity, data, security and operations teams all own a piece.

Retrieved text can inform, never authorise

The refund scenario is indirect prompt injection. The attacker never talks to the agent; they plant instructions in a source the agent will read. Her design question is sharp and practical: who can write to the knowledge sources your agent retrieves from? Detection helps, she says, but you still need controls beyond the model, because the next question is whose authority the agent is running on.

She lays out three identity patterns: delegated access on behalf of a signed-in user (the agent inherits that user's reach), an agent with its own account like a digital worker, and app-only identities for background work. If any of these is broad, a fooled model gets broad reach.

MCP is a protocol, not a trust decision

The Model Context Protocol section is the one platform teams will screenshot. MCP standardises how agents discover and call tools, which is convenient. It doesn't make a server trustworthy. Her example shows a ticket-search tool whose description quietly asks the model to send a report elsewhere, which is tool description poisoning. Review servers and tool definitions, restrict discovery, validate requests and enforce permissions at execution.

Then the line every agent builder should tape to the monitor: capability doesn't mean authorization. Writing "please don't delete data" in the system prompt is a suggestion. A policy check in the application that denies the delete because no approver exists, and logs the attempt, is a boundary.

Follow the attack, then follow the trace

Cynthia connects the pieces into one path: the agent retrieves the poisoned policy, mistakes it for an instruction, tries the export, and the API rejects it. The model was fooled; the system held. Controls sit at several points (inputs, retrieved context, tool arguments, actions, outputs), and an AI gateway is a good shared front door for model traffic, but tool execution may take a different route to an enterprise API and still needs its own check.

Correlated traces let the security team see the denied export even when the customer sees a normal answer. Her case study uses the Microsoft stack she works in, including Entra Agent ID and Agent 365 for agent identity and life cycle, as one example of turning these principles into platform capabilities.

Least agency

Her closing pattern is least agency: enough freedom to do the job and no more, narrow tool access, deny unapproved actions by default, humans in the loop for irreversible changes, and deterministic application logic validating whatever the model proposes. Before production, ask who owns the agent, which identity it uses, and whether you can trace, stop and recover its actions.

Who should watch

Engineers moving from chatbots to agents with tools, and security architects reviewing them. It's a clear, structured talk rather than a code walkthrough, and the refund story makes it easy to retell in your own design review.

entry.title: Physical AI safety agents should reason over a system graph
entry.summary: Vraj Patel of Apptronik at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026 on bounded agents, system graphs and skills for safety assurance in robots and AVs.
entry.content:
Robots and autonomous vehicles keep changing after they ship, and the safety case has to keep up with every new perception model. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026, Vraj Patel, Staff Systems Engineer at Apptronik and formerly at May Mobility, showed how bounded, human-supervised agents can help with continuous safety assurance, as long as they reason over an explicit system graph instead of a loose pile of documents.

His thesis is that a prompt alone isn't enough here. The context has to be engineered first. Vraj presented in his individual professional capacity, and the framework he showed is illustrative rather than a specific employer's system.

The documents outpace the engineers

Building a humanoid, an autonomous mobile robot or an AV produces engineering docs, safety analyses, prototypes, hypotheses and evidence at a pace that grows as teams lean on tools like Claude and Codex. The material ends up fragmented across tools. An agent pointed at that mess will happily produce plausible safety claims. Vraj's answer is to give it four pillars to stand on: a system graph, skills, tools and data, and governance with approvals.

Build the graph before the prompt

The system graph starts with the operational design domain (ODD): where the system works, whether a warehouse, a city limit or a construction site, and under which conditions, such as rain or sunlight. From there it maps objects and interactions, hazards (especially to humans), safety goals, requirements, verification criteria and finally claims. Edges carry relations such as "mitigates a hazard" or "is verifiable", so the graph bounds where an agent can wander.

The sources stay whatever teams already use: Jama or Doors for requirements, Draw.io or Miro for architecture, Confluence and Jira for docs, Git for releases. The abstract keeps the model-based systems engineering (MBSE) model as the single source of truth, with frameworks such as ISO 26262, ISO 21448 (SOTIF), UL 4600 and ASPICE as guides.

Skills with golden cases

Vraj shows a hazard coverage skill as a template: a triggering condition, inputs, the procedure the agent runs, and an output (JSON or Markdown) where every item carries a unique ID. The guideline baked in: never override, never claim safety without human approval. Each skill gets golden cases to evaluate against.

His worked scenario is a person cutting into the path of a moving unit after the perception model is revised. The agent detects what changed in the model, finds the impacted scenarios, hazards and controls, checks coverage and whether other systems are affected, and escalates if the safety scenarios need a rerun. In his words on the slide, the outcome is a traceable question for an engineer, not an autonomous safe-to-release verdict.

Agents are software that can fail

The point that will land with anyone who has written a safety case: treat the agent workload itself as something that needs its own safety case. Measure evidence validity, false positive rate, classification quality, tool compliance and reviewer acceptance. The abstract names the risks to watch: hallucinated evidence, incomplete context, prompt drift and over-automation.

Human authority is an architectural requirement here. Agents can read and retrieve; they can't write or override without a person signing off, and whoever approves the output owns it. "The AI did it" is not an accountable party.

Start with one vertical slice

The roadmap is refreshingly modest. Build a small graph for one vertical, connect the sources, ship one skill, evaluate it, harden it, then expand. His three takeaways: engineer the context, package the procedure, and command the action. Traceability from evidence to decision to claim is the core competency the standards ask for anyway.

Who should watch

Systems and safety engineers in robotics, AVs and other physical AI, plus anyone building agents for regulated engineering workflows. It's an architecture talk with no live demo, and the system graph is the part worth sketching on your own whiteboard.
